subsubtopic: SUGGESTION THAT GOVERNMENT SHOULD CHANGE ITS POLICIES-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, business investment is plunging downward in response to dwindling company profits. The National Energy Program, the Foreign Investment Review Agency, and the disastrous MacEachen budgets, with the resultant high interest rate policies, have ravaged the business community in Canada with the obvious result of one and one third million unemployed, thousands of bankruptcies, and the loss of homes by hundreds of families. The latest Gallup poll indicates a mere 14 per cent of Canadians think the government is doing well with the economy. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid):
That the government inform the uninformed 14 per cent, who obviously have neither read a paper, listened to a radio, nor watched television, so that they, too, as well as the 86 per cent, will realize just how badly the Liberal government has mishandled the economy, or, better still, that the government immediately change the direction of its present disastrous policies.

line employees entered into a three-year contract in September, 1981, and these employees have been advised that their contract will be cancelled and the 6 per cent restraint will take over on September 1, 1982. If this arrangement follows through, it will be making flesh of one and fish of another. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart):
That the government be consistent and permit every contract to run to completion before applying the restraint program.

speechtext:

COMMONS DEBATES___________________July 26, 1982
Oral Questions

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. Over the weekend the minister said on the CTV program "Question Period" that the program for cheaper loans for home owners, farmers, and small businessmen will be in operation by October, and that he cannot imagine circumstances which would prevent the implementation of this program. Is this statement based on the preliminary reaction of the special consultative committee, or is it based on work that is being done within his department?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I do not recall saying anything about the month of October. I have noticed in press accounts that that date is put on the time when the program might be implemented. 1 have not had an opportunity to check the transcript but, in any event, what I said is based upon my own expectations. As I stated on the program, I still cannot imagine circumstances which would put this program off the rails. I have confidence that the committee will find it acceptable or, indeed, if the committee wants to make further recommendations, 1 believe it will find it to be a program which can be implemented. However, I have not received any report from that committee yet, nor do I have an additional report from my department.

Madam Speaker, my supplementary question is also directed to the Minister of Finance. 1 am sure the minister is aware there has been some discussion in the media about some substantial technical problems relating to the implementation of the program. There is also some question that the projected cost of the program as set out in the budget will be far less than what will be the case once the program is implemented.
1 want to ask the minister whether he took these factors fully into account in the answer he gave to my first question and in his comments at the weekend when he made the statement that the program will be implemented in a very short period of time.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I did notice at the weekend that concerns raised by unidentified persons as to the operation or feasibility of this program were summarized. I believe that is a healthy process because the purpose of the consultation is to ensure that all the possible technical difficulties are examined and that a way is found to implement the program. I have had no further reports either from the committee or from my department to justify the comments the hon. member quoted.

Madam Speaker, it would certainly be helpful to Canadians to know whether the minister takes seriously the concerns which have been expressed, and whether he feels the program will sail through as he indicated at the weekend.

Madam Speaker, 1 think the minister must also be aware that there is some serious concern in the financial community that the indexed form of investment will provide formidable competition to Canada Savings Bonds and other forms of savings instruments, none of which have the benefit of this indexed feature. In addition to being considerable competition, it may well push up interest rates on general mortgages on existing houses. If the committee reaches the same conclusion, does the minister intend to reassess the plan, or is he considering changing the form of Canada Savings Bonds to provide an indexed feature on them so that they can compete with the new indexed term deposit?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I note that the hon. member used the expression that these proposed indexed instruments would provide formidable competition. Certainly it is intended that they be attractive so that depositors will move large amounts of funds into such indexed instruments. Unless they are attractive, or indeed strongly competitive, then the plan would be unworkable. Offhand, I do not find that a compelling deficiency in the plan. It seems to me that it must be made attractive to depositors and holders of large amounts of funds in other forms for them to move those funds into indexed instruments.

Have any members of the government been in touch with CN Rail and asked it to temper its demands, which appear to be in direct defiance of the 6 per cent ceiling on which the

subsubtopic: DEMAND FOR TARIFF CHANGES IN EXCESS OF SIX PER CENT

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF CONTROL PROGRAM ON WAGE SETTLEMENTS
speechtext:

From newspaper reports I understand that the minister was in the room with the Prime Minister and Mr. Sinclair when the Prime Minister invited Mr. Sinclair to be head of this blue blood private sector industry committee to help the government out of its difficulties.
How in the world could the public have any credibility in Mr. Sinclair if there were no discussions, not about rates which CP would be charging its customers that might be above the 6 per cent or 5 per cent suggestion of the government, but about contracts already negotiated by CP Rail, and I understand also by CP Air employees, when CN employees, let alone Air Canada ones, will have a negotiated and/or enforced 6 per cent and 5 per cent increase which is far below what CP has already negotiated? Was there any discussion that, as a moral leader in this difficult situation, Mr. Sinclair would go to his people in CP and show another example of leadership by having CP roll back some of the increases?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: EFFECT OF CONTROL PROGRAM ON WAGE SETTLEMENTS

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF CONTROL PROGRAM ON WAGE SETTLEMENTS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, that is an interesting answer by the Minister of Finance because I remember when he had some interest in labour matters in the House of Commons. Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Transport. Recently radio licence fees for private aircraft were doubled. Both landing fees and parking rates have been increased to ridiculous levels, yet on July 1, as the hon. member for Vancouver South pointed out on Friday, the Vancouver airport shut down vfr traffic in the middle of the day. Madam Speaker, recently I had a question on the Vancouver incident of July 1. SUGGESTION THAT PUBLIC SERVICE OFFER SIX-MONTH JOBS IN GASPfe AREA

Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul J. Cosgrove (Minister of Public Works):

subsubtopic: CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION RENTAL UNITS-APPLICATION OF CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I assume that the motivation for the question arises from the announcement of the government on budget evening. I would refer the hon. member to a news release issued by the President of the Treasury Board, and which is dated July 20. I indicated that Public Works Canada, all agencies reporting through me to Parliament, have agreed to comply with the government policy.

subsubtopic: CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION RENTAL UNITS-APPLICATION OF CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext: That was a very interesting answer.

Do you know the answer?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance and Acting Prime Minister. On Friday, July 16, four of the Acting Prime Minister's colleagues, the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Justice, and the Secretary of State, flew to St. John's, Newfoundland, in a government jet to attempt an impossible task. They said they were going to sell the new federal budget.
They had a press conference at 11.30 and had 250 people whom they invited in to drinks and lunch in the middle of the day at the Holiday Inn, at a cost of $4,700 for that little face-to-face meeting. Is it the government's policy to sell restraint in this manner, by a show of opulence, wealth, and power, with two bars in a Holiday Inn, and glazed salmon, just like the minister's eyes are glazed now. Is this how the minister plans to sell restraint in the government to the Canadian people, or will the government cancel these ostentatious and opulent shows? Will the minister tell us how many of these there will be, and at how many places does the government plan to have such a performance across Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think the ostentation and opulence are probably more in the hon. member's mind and imagination than existed at the event which was hosted in St. John's by my colleagues. In any event, if the hon. member is really concerned about restraint as it applies to public expenditures, I think I can assure him that whatever was spent will not be picked up by the Canadian taxpayer.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Minister of National Revenue was asked a question there about the general public's fear that the new budget might not work. He said fear is good as long as it is not paralysing fear. Let me tell you I am paralysed with fear when I look at the Acting Prime Minister.
The press has been told that this $4,700 bill from the Holiday Inn for drinks, glazed salmon, booze, wines, hams and all the rest of it, was paid for by the Liberal Party of Canada. Would the Acting Prime Minister confirm whether or not these bills are to be met by the Liberal Party of Canada? If they are, why are these ministers travelling by government aircraft and who is paying for the aircraft? What is going on? Is this a show of the Liberal Party, or is the public paying for it? Who is paying for it, and why? Would he explain just what is happening and tell the public what the Liberal Party and the government are doing, or is there any way of distinguishing one from the other?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member has no business inquiring into the affairs of the Liberal Party. He is entitled to inquire as to whether the taxpayers paid for this particular event. The taxpayers did not.
Who paid for the aircraft?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: The hon. member talks about not being impressed by the Acting Prime Minister.
Paralysed with fear.

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: I suggest that he not become over confident. Every time that happens to him, he falls hard.

subsubtopic: CAPPING OF PENSIONS UNDER CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. Does the minister still fully intend to see the remuneration under the Canadian Armed Forces pension plan capped at 6 per cent next year, bearing in mind that last year
July 26, 1982

the receipts and credits to the Canadian Forces superannuation account amounted to $480 million in interest alone, at 5 per cent, and the pay-out to servicemen and beneficiaries was only $280 million? Does the Minister of National Defence feel that it is fair to cap these indexed pensions for which servicemen have been promised full indexing at the cost of living rate-to cap them at 6 per cent, bearing in mind that the pension account is $200 million in surplus for last year when you compare accrued interest with funds paid out to beneficiaries?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: CAPPING OF PENSIONS UNDER CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext: Madam Speaker, this is a question which will have to be evaluated by the Treasury Board and our department. I think it would only be fair if we succeed in our program of 6 and 5, if the inflation rate goes down to 6 and 5 in one or two years. I think the indexation of pensions has always been subject to our cost of living inflation rates. If they go down to 6 and 5 I think it would only be fair to index these pensions to the rate of inflation at the time.

subsubtopic: CAPPING OF PENSIONS UNDER CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext: The minister knows that if this undertaking is carried out, the government will have broken trust with the servicemen of Canada.

subsubtopic: CAPPING OF PENSIONS UNDER CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the Solicitor General. In the same light, if we look at the Royal Canadian Mounted Police superannuation account we find that contributions by the members of the RCMP amounted to $22.5 million in the last fiscal year, but beneficiaries received only $16 million, and interest accredited to the account amounted to $60 million at a rate of 6 per cent. Is it fair to cap the pensions at a six per cent increase, remembering that members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have been promised full cost of living indexing, and recognizing that the pay-outs to the beneficiaries are far short of interest and contributions from serving members of the RCMP?

subsubtopic: CAPPING OF PENSIONS UNDER CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as the Minister of Finance has often indicated, we are seeking to establish a 6 and 5 per cent inflation rate for the Canadian economy over the next two years. In the area where the federal government has direct control and can show leadership, we are proposing to do so with the support of the House.

subtopic: PROGRESS IN ESTABLISHING NEW NATIONAL SECURITY SERVICE
PROGRESS IN ESTABLISHING NEW NATIONAL SECURITY SERVICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is also for the Solicitor General. On August 25, I believe it will be a year since Mr. Fred Gibson, Q.C., was appointed head of the planning and transition group to develop
Oral Questions
a new security and intelligence service. What progress, if any, has been made during this long interval? What can the minister tell the House?

subtopic: PROGRESS IN ESTABLISHING NEW NATIONAL SECURITY SERVICE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, a considerable study has been done of the problems of national security which were the basis of the McDonald Commission's recommendations. A document is in the process of preparation for me to take to my cabinet colleagues, I am looking forward, in the next few months, to being able to spend a considerable amount of time with them on the consideration of national security matters, and hope that it would be possible some time in the fall to bring forward the government's response to the recommendations.

Madam Speaker, have any new guidelines been formulated, even if not publicized, to clarify the role of existing personnel in the force during this transition period, in order to reassure them and the country about their future and to prevent loss of some special expertise?

Yes, Madam Speaker. Mr. Gibson and the commissioner, and the deputy commissioner responsible for national security, have been in constant touch with the members of the security service assuring them of a continued place in the security service and it will be the basis of the new separated security service when one is formed.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: USE OF GOVERNMENT LEVERAGE IN APPLICATION OF CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Acting Prime Minister will know that the Prime Minister said on Friday, "I would hope that every grant, every accord and every subsidy that the government is paying out of taxpayers' money would be used as leverage to enforce the 6 and 5 provision." Is it the policy of the government that every grant, every accord and every subsidy of the federal government will be used as leverage?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: USE OF GOVERNMENT LEVERAGE IN APPLICATION OF CONTROL PROGRAM
speechtext: Yes, Madam Speaker, that is the intention.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, have guidelines been established, or are they being established?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the cabinet is presently engaged in the process of preparing these guidelines. We

July 26, 1982
Oral Questions
have already had discussions. The general principle has been established, and we will be approving these specific guidelines probably this week.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, will those guidelines be published so that people who are taking advantage of government programs will know in advance of any unstated strings that might be attached to any grants, any accord, any subsidy-any strings attached which are unstated and which are not in accord with the law of the land?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, we have not given any consideration to the question of publication, but the Leader of the Opposition will recall that when we did establish certain guidelines for administered prices, the President of the Treasury Board did make these public. I would think that, once we have completed our work, we will give consideration to whether it would be useful to make those criteria or guidelines public.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, there is enough confusion in the country right now. It would be absolutely incredible and verging on the criminal for the government to have this kind of guideline and not let the people know when they apply for subsidies, accords or grants from the Government of Canada. Let me ask the Deputy Prime Minister whether this new policy will apply retroactively. Will it apply to people who are now in receipt of grants, accords or subsidies from the Government of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it would be my opinion that it would not be justified to review all former grants which were put forward or put out under particular circumstances. This is a policy which was established in the budget. We are determined, insofar as we can bring it about, to establish a 6 per cent and 5 per cent economy. Where we are giving grants or incentives, we intend to enter into discussions and into negotiations with the recipients, encouraging and persuading them to follow the 6 per cent and 5 per cent rule. That will be our policy and our effort. Nothing will be done in a way which is not in accordance with the 6 per cent and 5 per cent rule, and nothing will be done which is not in accordance with the public interest and the welfare of the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATION-GRANTS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, an interesting aspect of the explanation to this House might revolve around whether the government at one time appointed the chief executive officer of Imperial Oil to advise the government on competition while the company was skinning the country. Again, an explanation of the appointment of Ian Sinclair to the government's blue ribbon committee might be interesting.
However, I would like to ask the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs whether he could explain how he proposes to remove the income bias from the urea formaldehyde foam insulation program which would allow upper income families to receive the $5,000 grant while lower income families would be deprived of it by the nature and structure of the program. In order to facilitate movement, I think it would be valuable for the minister to give us some indication of how he thinks that bias might be removed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATION-GRANTS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the interpretation of the hon. member is misleading. It is quite clear that the program applies to everyone, irrespective of income. It has been brought to our attention, and it is obvious, that some people might have more difficulty in taking advantage of the program. This weekend, during a meeting with the National Advisory Council, I undertook to find ways to help these people. Indeed, the home owners' representatives who met with me this weekend have indicated that they want to work through a sub-committee of their own in order to address these very questions. Possibly, additional funds could come from the provinces. Now that we know the result of the board of review, we will indeed try to bring the private sector in for some compensation. At the same time, we will explore other federal government programs which could be beneficial to home owners. So, there are a variety of ways by which to help the home owners who have difficulties, but the very first thing which must be done is to pass the legislation now before the House, which would at least entitle every home owner to the possibility of receiving the minimum of $5,000.

subsubtopic: UREA FORMALDEHYDE FOAM INSULATION-GRANTS TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I think that this is probably one of the truly momentous occasions when the minister has completely reversed himself, as he now admits that this is the minimum amount to be payable. In case he has slipped, perhaps he can clarify the matter for me.

Madam Speaker, the minister is certainly correct when he says the bill should be quickly moved through the House. But is he asking to create a situation, as a result of that legislation, where $5,000 would be immediately mailed out to upper income families who have the money to clear the urea formaldehyde foam out of their
July 26, 1982

homes, while senior citizens who are experiencing health problems and who do not have the money to remove the foam from their homes would be forced to wait until advisory committees, the private sector or other people come up with some money somewhere down the line? Would the minister like me to vote for a program which would give $5,000 to upper-income families and would not give the money to lower-income families in Canada? Would he like that?
Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate
Affairs): Madam Speaker, the hon. member could vote one way or he could vote the other. I will not tell him how to vote. But I am telling him, however, that he has been putting pressure on members of the National Advisory Council who have met with me to try to change their decision unanimously to support the passage of this legislation.
Shame!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Indeed, I would hope that in the coming hours the hon. member will not deny thousands of home owners the opportunity to receive the grants of $5,000 which are available to them. When I refer to the minimum of $5,000 for those who have gone through major expenditures and are spending more than $5,000, I use that expression that, indeed, they will be receiving this amount of money. We are on record as trying to find additional funds from the provinces, from the private sector and, if possible, from the federal government from other programs to help these home owners to get rid of the foam, if that is their desire, and to apply the corrective measures to their homes. I do hope the hon. member will stop bargaining with some of the representatives of the home owners and will indeed support this legislation.

Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Communications. The Privy Council Office agenda on Friday listed an extension of the term of employment of the co-chairmen of the federal cultural policy review committee to December 31, 1982. Could the minister tell the House when the final report of that commission is expected, since it was expected in September? If the report is delayed, as the extension would suggest, until some time in November or December, what will that do, in particular, to the minister's broadcasting policy?

Madam Speaker, a week or two ago I was advised by the co-chairmen of the review committee, both Mr. Applebaum and Mr. Hebert, that they did not expect to be in a position to make their report public until the end of October. So, I would expect that the report would indeed be made public some time after that date. The extension was granted until the end of December in the event that there were some unforeseen delays in the
Oral Questions
publication. Obviously, before the government would want to finalize any broadcasting strategy, and I do underline the word "finalize", the government would want to have the benefit of the views of the Applebaum-Hebert Commission.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):

speakeroldname: Mr. Ian Deans (for Mr. Skelly) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 1
July 23, 1982-That Bill C-92, an act to amend the National Harbours Board Act, the Government Harbours and Piers Act, the Harbour Commissions Act, the Canada Shipping Act and the Fishing and Recreational Harbours Act, be amended in Clause 2 adding immediately after line 17 at page 3 the following:
"(/) shall, where possible, attempt to complement the development of a
Canadian marine industrial strategy."

Madam Speaker, this motion follows very closely an amendment we presented in committee which asks that the bill have an additional objective. In committee we had asked that there be a specific statement which encourages Canadian traffic to move through Canadian ports. We thought this was most important because it is common knowledge that there is a good deal of Canadian traffic now going through American ports which should be going through Canadian ports. That was voted down in committee and we asked that it be added.
We now have an amendment from the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) which states that the port policy shall, where possible, attempt to complement the development of the Canadian marine industrial strategy. Members of this House surely know that it is the position of this party, and I would hope of all parties, that the time is long overdue when we must develop our own shipping to a much greater degree. Most of our ships are not built in Canada or manned by Canadians. Quite frequently, of course, it is ships of convenience which come into our ports and carry out goods at very reduced prices.
As part of a marine industrial strategy we feel very strongly that there must be training programs for people who want to get into the shipping industry. If you meet with marine unions and with the people who have had a long history on the docks and in the industry, they are all in their late middle age or older. It is really criminal, Mr. Speaker, that young people in
July 26, 1982

our country are not being trained in the necessary skills for the marine industry. In fact, many of our skilled people come from overseas. It is important that we have a positive program of shipbuilding. Space should be reserved for this in the development of our ports. There should be a real promotion of the shipbuilding industry. No longer do we want to see docks made in Japan with a subsidy from this government and then towed to the port of Vancouver. I support this amendment and I hope other parties will as well.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment in essence commends the support of everybody in this chamber. However, I have some reservation as to whether this is the proper bill under which it should be debated. In any event, the end sought by the amendment is commendable and should be given serious consideration by this government.
In the last three or four days 1 have attempted frequently to rise to ask the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) what the Japanese trade officials said to him when he put the specific question, as he alleges, as to who will transport our Canadian natural resources from our country to theirs and other Asian nations. In that case it refers specifically to gas, but there is also the question of coal.
When the government under the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) was defeated by the NDP and the reigning Liberal government, the then minister of transport, the distinguished hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), had gone 90 per cent of the way toward the gradual establishment of a merchant marine for Canada. It was then killed. It is dead.
The holier-than-thou attitude of my friends to the left seems to promote the development of a marine strategy for Canada to a very high level. They conveniently forget that just two short years ago the end they are now seeking to achieve would have been accomplished had they not got into bed with my friends across the way. That is just one example. I am sure dozens of members on this side of the House can cite amendments which, had they not got into a holy alliance two years ago, would now be effective. That end will I support without any question. Whatever the amendment in principle means, if it does mean the development of a maritime strategy for this country, it could only be supported and endorsed. Indeed, it has to be supported and endorsed. If it means greater safety, if there is some way we can use ports legislation to create an understanding and awareness of the need for greater safety and greater training, then by all means let us support it.
It is a matter of some regret that the member would use this ports legislation to bring in an amendment that should be dealt with somewhere else. It should be dealt with in direct confrontation with this government over its failure to establish a marine strategy for this country, to re-establish a Canadian merchant marine, to reinforce in the minds of Canadians and in statute the urgency of Canada getting back some of the $4 billion or $5 billion annually that goes offshore to foreign cartels for the movement of our goods and the importation of
Canada Ports Corporation Act
goods and services. It is bad enough when they are transported directly by water, and even worse when done indirectly through ports in the United States. I will not belabour that point.
In principle, the amendment directs itself to a very worthwhile principle. I am not sure that Bill C-92, to establish a national ports corporation and a series of local port corporations, is the vehicle to do it. However, it gives us an opportunity to shed a little light on what the sponsor of this amendment has been attempting to do in recent weeks. By all means it has that type of general endorsement and support.
The government has been remiss. The Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) more than any other in this chamber is perfectly aware of missed opportunities. Foreign vessels have been hauling natural resources out of our north such as paper, coal and gas. This is occurring day in and day out. These foreign-owned vessels are crewed by other than Canadians. In terms of wheat, this involves billions. Not a bushel leaves Canada on a Canadian-registered, Canadian-crewed, Canadian-owned vessel. Why not? Thousands of jobs are at stake. It is either an absence of vision or an absence of will.
I suspect it is that we fall prey to the difficulty that occurs from time to time in this chamber. When a good idea is put forward, if it does not come from the government it is rejected. It is amoral to have put aside the work of the former minister of transport, the hon. member for Vegreville, who had put in place the steps that would have led to the gradual development of a Canadian merchant marine and, therefore, the resolution of this problem, albeit this government has been preoccupied. However, why it has not put in place in recent years a new national transportation act, I will never understand.
We have 27 horses in front of a vehicle that does not exist. We are entering into a debate that will be over later today. For the most part, hon. members will be pleased when it is over. However, we have in front of us dozens of horses without a vehicle. It is not in tune with the realities of the world today. There is no vehicle to load or to pull. The National Transportation Act is outdated. Its principal opening statement is outdated. It does not meet the needs for the balance of this century.
I support the principle of the amendment. However, I have some doubt as to whether this is the proper place to deal with it. 1 commend the Johnnys-come-lately to my left for having thought to see some two years after the fact whether they did let the horse out of the barn by failing to close the door.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I certainly would like to thank my colleagues for allowing me this opportunity to slip through the door and make some comments. I would also like to offer my thanks for the somewhat off-centre support of the previous speaker.
1 recognize the job which was done in this sphere by the former minister of state for marine transportation and the former Conservative government, it is unfortunate that when a government is hanged, for whatever reasons, we generally lose some good programs with the bad. I was certainly a strong supporter of the previous government's efforts with regard to this particular matter, and 1 hope when this amendment is put that the Conservatives, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and the Liberal Party support it.
In my speech at second reading of this bill I mentioned that it was extremely important that we provide direction in this legislation to the administrators of ports so that they can begin to develop and enhance linkages with other functions in addition to direct port functions. When there are spin-offs from actions taken by administrators of ports, we should attempt to capture those spin-offs. In the bill we should provide policy guidance for administrators so that they can develop and enhance a marine industrial strategy. If we were to do that, I think we would be moving in a very positive direction.
There should also be policy statements in other legislative initiatives so that there can be linkage between one body and another. I suggest there may well be an opportunity to make that kind of statement in the Canagrex bill. However, suffice it to say that I would like to have an indication from the Minister of Transport that he is willing to accept the basic concept within this amendment.
1 would like to cite four examples of why administrative guidance in the bill is necessary. It basically would help to capture tens of thousands of jobs and enormous revenues associated with related or complementary marine industrial activities.
What really brought on this amendment was the recent announcement by Dome Petroleum that it would become involved in shipyard development on the west coast. While seeking support for the Rim gas project, Dome went up and down the west coast telling a number of communities that there would be a shipyard developed and that it would be used to build two of four proposed LNG carriers to carry natural gas to Japan from British Columbia. A year later, last Friday we saw in the newspapers that Dome Petroleum had been given the go ahead by the province of British Columbia, and Dome announced that the marine industrial activities related to this project would accrue to Japan. It was announced that not four carriers would be built, but five, and that all of them would likely be built in Japan. Each of those LNG carriers represents 2.5 million hours of employment. Just the containment system on one of those vessels would put 400 individuals to work for two and a half years. We are giving up an enormous number of jobs, about 2,000, for two and a half years on just that one order.
We must understand that a drydock is part of a port facility. It is part of the interplay and the organic growth between ports and other allied functions. Dome Petroleum decided last year that it wanted to build a drydock for the Beaufort Sea. That project was bid on by a Vancouver company, but Dome decided it would be better built in Japan and those jobs were created offshore. Dome Petroleum is an example of a company into which the federal government is putting tremendous amounts of taxpayers' money, yet Dome is selling off resources at fire sale prices. The industrial spin-offs are going to Japan, basically, and that is wrong.
In the administration and development of ports it is imperative that the administrators be given policy guidance and that benefits be captured for Canadians in the placement and development of other marine activities which enhance or relate to a certain port.
The second example I would like to cite is the case of the port at Prince Rupert. That port involves Federal Commerce and Navigation and the National Harbours Board. Federal Commerce and Navigation will be shipping coal to Japan in four large bulk carriers. Federal Commerce and Navigation, a Canadian company, in conjunction with the National Harbours Board and a number of others, will be developing this project and receiving government funds and assistance. However, on the other side of the coin, two of those four large bulk carriers will be built in Korea and the other two in Belgium. That is absolutely ridiculous in terms of an economic strategy. What has happened, basically, is that the government has given up, or given away by default, tens of thousands of jobs associated with this, plus the revenue which would accrue.
Today in the House and every day for the past week statements have been made by hon. members on all sides of the House which have indicated a sincere commitment. These statements have not been Johnny-come-lately statements. There is tremendous potential in the marine industrial development field and the government must act on it.
CP Ships has to be the most blatant example of contempt for Canadians. Today there was a rather crude attempt to bootleg a question into this House. I wonder how the government can explain the appointment of Ian Sinclair, the chief executive officer of Canadian Pacific, to lead the Canadian economy out of the Liberal wilderness. One of the subsidiaries of CP has 40 ships which it will not register in Canada. These ships carry Canadian goods to and from many parts of the world. About 1,500 to 2,000 jobs are directly associated with those ships. They have British officers and foreign crews. The money they earn from transporting goods is deposited in Bermuda to avoid the payment of tax. To my way of thinking that is absolutely unscrupulous, and to appoint Ian Sinclair as economic adviser lacks any wisdom whatsoever.
We have the same problem with Federal Commerce and Navigation. That company will be involved with Dome in the Arctic Pilot Project. There will be four LNG carriers which will have state of the art equipment. They will have cold-temperature steel and ice-hardened hulls, and they will be working in Arctic areas. If that project goes ahead with those
July 26, 1982

two companies, because of their very poor track records and the absolute vacuum in government policy in this area, the result will be that those four carriers will probably be built in Finland or some other European country.
Just to recap, it is imperative that this government get off its hands and begin to shape and develop a marine industrial strategy. It seems that the government is absolutely oblivious to the fact that important benefits are being given away. The Department of Finance, the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Transport are all involved. The Department of Fisheries and Oceans is involved, as is the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. All these departments seem to be working at cross-purposes. There does not seem to be a sense of policy direction. Each department has its own goals and, unfortunately, in the competitive building of their empires we wind up with the chaos in the marine industries we have today. We are selling off resources at fire sale prices. Ships to carry Canadian goods are being built in foreign countries.
The proposal we have put forward is a needed change. The previous speaker spoke of the initiatives his government took. This government has taken no taken initiatives, and because of the latest insult by Dome Petroleum to the people of the west coast, we have written to every municipality on the coast of British Columbia asking that they pass resolutions and send telegrams to this government deploring its failure to fill this policy vacuum. We have written to every marine industrial union, every marine operating union and every shipbuilder asking them to pass the same kinds of resolutions and to send them to the Premier of British Columbia and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau). We have asked them to appoint representatives who can come together in a meeting to develop a steering committee. We have asked them to form a common front lobbying organization to meet face to face with the Premier of British Columbia and his ministers and bureaucrats-who are in competition within the same government- and to demand action on this issue. Once that is resolved provincially, they should come to Ottawa and confront the Prime Minister with the problem of the loss of jobs in British Columbia and confront these ministers and bureaucrats as well. They will come, because tens of thousands of British Columbians are out of work. They need that employment, Mr. Speaker. The province is roughly $1 billion in the hole. It virtually amounts to negligence to give away those sources of revenue, without even taking into account the revenue that would accrue to Canada as a whole.
It is vitally important to develop a marine industrial strategy to capture those benefits. It is unfortunate that the people who are working and who are busy must expend their resources on such massive efforts to convince governments of what is obvious.
This should be happening in other regions of the country as well. The Atlantic region should be forming a common front
Canada Ports Corporation Act
organization to lobby the provinces and the federal government. In Quebec by 1983 two shipyards will lay off 2,000 people because the order books are empty beyond that time and they will lose jobs to foreigners. In Ontario there is the same kind of problem. In the House the hon. member for St. Catharines (Mr. Reid) has appealed to the government for action on many occasions. Unfortunately, members on the government side continue to tell us about the office of industrial benefits. The last time they told us about this grand initiative they compared it to the offshore supply office in Great Britain in which thousands of people are involved. And the last time we were told about Canada's initiative, 24 people were involved in projecting this two or three decades into the next century.
The Canada Oil and Gas Act was held up because it is pitifully weak. The manpower procurement section was hopeless, as was the provision to capture the industrial spin-off. Eventually, in order to resolve the impasse, when we realized that the ministers would not strengthen the provisions in the legislation, we settled for their appearing before the committee, in camera, to explain the mechanisms they would use to develop and capture those industrial benefits. They came up with the invention of the office of industrial benefits, but it does not have any direct authority, nor the human or financial resources to carry out a mandate such as is before us today.
If the government chooses to respond to this, I would plead with it not to use those ludicrous examples of government initiative. I implore the government to present a marine industrial strategy, a mechanism by which we can capture the benefits which we are literally giving away by default to the Asians and Europeans.
1 urge members of the House to accept the amendment that I have put forward, Mr. Speaker. It does not in any way hamper the thrust of the bill but simply asks the administrators of Canadian ports, whenever possible, to enhance other benefits that result from their activities and to make a slight effort to capture them.
There is another example we could use in order to bring to shore ships owned by Canadian companies but registered in foreign countries and sailed by foreign crews. The United Nations commission on trade and development advocated the adoptions of a resolution by all member nations that would provide for 40 per cent of the exports and imports of a country being carried in its own flagships. The trading partner would carry the other 40 per cent and 20 per cent would be available to itinerant carriers.
If we were to adopt that resolution and insist that our 40 per cent be carried in Canadian bottoms and, if there were no Canadian hulls available, that our trading partners be given our share of the trade for future consideration, then an opportunity would exist to allow those Canadian-owned foreign registered vessels one year's grace to be registered in Canada and carry Canadian crews. After that year of grace, they would then forever hold their peace. They would then be on the lowest priority for any Canadian cargo coming or going to

July 26, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
this country. They would have to wait until Canadian registered ships were filled, then the ships of our trading partners, then any others and then their vessels would be eligible.
Unfortunately, the government has not put that policy in position. But if the government would adopt the UNCTAD resolution and insist on a one-year grace period with no taxation benefits and no incentives-either bring the Canadian ships to shore or do not carry Canadian cargoes-there would be a stampede to develop a Canadian merchant fleet.

Mr. Speaker, first, I would like to say a few words to thank the members of the Committee on Transport and Communications who worked very hard on Bill C-92, and had quite a few meetings in addition to their regular schedule. I therefore wish to express my gratitude.

In the committee report amendments have been made to nine clauses and sometimes there was more than one amendment per clause. These amendments are often of a technical nature and a few are of a substantive or quasi-substantive nature. For example, the contributions made by the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) and the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) to Clause 13(32) with respect to the tabling of the annual report and its automatic reference to the standing committee and the automatic reference of ministerial directives to the standing committee are of a rather substantive nature.
1 might underline that there are not only government amendments but two are from the New Democratic Party, from the hon. member for Regina West and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell), three are from the Progressive Conservative Party, one from the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East, and two from the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook).
The government has already indicated that it is prepared to accept the committee report in its entirety as well as a number of amendments which will be introduced at this stage of the proceedings this afternoon.
Nevertheless, I should like to reject the first one, not that the motion is not worthwhile in its attempt to "complement the development of a Canadian marine industrial strategy". That is a very good idea. There is no doubt that any industrial strategy in any sector needs to be complemented. One agrees with that almost from the point of departure-
Then why don't you do it?

I don't think we should spend the afternoon talking only about a deep sea fleet for Canada, which is only one aspect of a marine industrial strategy. I do not think we should become obsessed with this single issue which, though important, is not the main purpose of this afternoon's debate.
As the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) knows, an industrial strategy is not to be found in a single bill; it is to be found in a body of laws, regulations and practices
which together constitutes an industrial strategy. This afternoon we are attending to the ports' aspect of this marine industrial strategy. Another day we will deal with coastal trade, another day with customs and another day with other aspects.
We will both be in the Senate by then!

I do not intend to go. This intention is a good one but, as my friend from Dartmouth-Halifax East has said, this is neither the time nor the place for it. I think we should concentrate on the bill at hand.
Another point I want to make is that the debate, which has taken place now over almost ten years, and particularly in the last two years, and the extensive consultations which have taken place, have not been on the deep sea fleet; they have been on ports policy. So my hon. friend is sort of sidetracking the main issue when he brings in this amendment on deep sea shipping. As my hon. friend knows, and he knows a good number of things, some of the ideas he has introduced this afternoon do not enjoy a very wide consensus in Canada today. There is quite a lot of division, particularly in his province, over these matters. So to come in now and introduce this as a major objective of Bill C-92 would be, in my view, divisive. As of now, most of the bill we have in front of us has been received in a mood of conciliation, so I think we should keep it that way. Consequently we on this side, Mr. Speaker, will vote against the motion.

Mr. Speaker, I find myself on the horns of a dilemma with this particular amendment, because if there is anything I dislike doing it is to encourage the "Liberal Party West", the NDP, when they come up with a good idea, because it does encourage them in other socialist thinking. However, the basic wording of the motion is something almost like motherhood, and nobody can disagree with that.
Then I have the dilemma of finding myself almost in agreement with the minister when he says the motion does not belong in the ports bill. I certainly do not want to encourage him either. However, when I look at this amendment and see that it is really one of those motherhood statements to the effect that we should have a marine policy in Canada, I do not think anyone disagrees with that. It is the right idea but is certainly in the wrong place. It has no business whatsoever being in the ports bill.
This bill deals with the administration of a port, but it does lead into any number of things. One of them, of course, is the terrible lack of action by this Liberal government in terms of an over-all ports transportation policy.
As an example, Mr. Speaker, why does the province of British Columbia find it necessary to import all of its liquor stocks for the Liquor Control Board of British Columbia through ports in Texas? I think part of the answer, of course, is perhaps a bit of shrinkage, if I may use that word, which
July 26, 1982

may take place on the docks. Nevertheless, that is legitimate business for the port of Vancouver or Prince Rupert.
Another example: why does a considerable amount of imports bound for Ontario come through the port of Oakland? Very simply, because the American railways have better transportation policies than this government has, and as a result it is cheaper to do it that way than to bring it into Vancouver, employ Canadians and use the Canadian rail system.
Quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) has made a nice statement, but it does not go far enough because it does not deal with the total transportation complex in Canada. For that matter, neither does the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). He is so worried about the flak he is getting over VIA Rail, so worried about trying to maintain his power in terms of the control and operation of the ports in this country, that he really does not have the time to sit down and say, hey, how come this great nation at one point had one of the largest merchant fleets in the world, the fourth largest navy, but today we have difficulty getting a couple of corvettes ready to go to sea? The merchant marine has totally disappeared, at a cost of literally hundreds of thousands of jobs.
The hon. member is absolutely correct when he talks about $6 billion worth of wheat shipped out of Canada in foreign bottoms. 1 am not suggesting that we do not sell wheat unless it is shipped in a Canadian bottom, but I am suggesting that he is quite correct when he talks about percentages. We are probably the only major exporter in the world which does not have some kind of firm policy and legislation which says: "If you want our wheat, we are delighted to sell it to you, but a percentage"-whether it is 30 per cent, 40 per cent or 60 per cent-"must be transported in Canadian ships." The same thing applies to all other exports from this country. The same thing applies to the vast amount of material we import. A percentage must be in Canadian bottoms. This would revitalize the whole industry right off the bat.
As far as shipbuilding is concerned, when I look at the losses this government has suffered at the expense of the Canadian people in any number of wild schemes-Atomic Energy of Canada for one, where they lose money even if they sell something-surely to goodness there is absolutely no excuse for the literally thousands and thousands of shipyard workers being out of jobs with no hope of getting them. I have seen the shipbuilding ways on the west coast; they are empty and they should not be empty. There is no reason why something should not be built there. There is no reason why shipbuilding in Canada could not become a major industry. The answer I generally get to the question of shipbuilding in Canada is that the Koreans work cheaper, that the Japanese are more efficient with different and better technology in shipbuilding. Whatever happened to Canadian inventiveness, Mr. Speaker? Whatever happened to Canadian gumption? We did it for a lot of years and very efficiently, but we are not doing it now. We should be doing it.
I have talked to any number of sailors who would like to sail on a Canadian ship. The hon. member mentioned the CPR and
Canada Ports Corporation Act
their 40 ships under flags of convenience. The flag of convenience ships flying the flag of Liberia or Panama are really a blot on Canadian shipping and they deprive Canadians of jobs unnecessarily. I say unnecessarily because, again, although something is just slightly cheaper if done some other way, if you had to do it in the way we are suggesting, through a Canadian ship, then of course you might just have to be considerably more efficient.
I support the hon. member for Comox-Powell River on the thrust of his amendment, but 1 do not think it belongs in the ports bill. It belongs in a real transportation policy statement, which should also include the railways and their utilization in shipping goods from the ports to their destination. It should include the Great Lakes, and should include an over-all industrial plan of one kind or another. We do not have any such thing. I wonder if there is anyone in the Department of Transport who even thinks about it once in a while. The minister nods his head; he says they think about it once in a while. Get some of their thoughts on paper and bring them back to the House so we can have a good look at them and perhaps develop something, so that eventually we can get these things unified to work in the best interests of all Canadians.
I am supporting the hon. member for Comox-Powell River. I think it is the right idea in the wrong place, but why not? Does it really make any difference? The proposed amendment is meaningless, but why not?

Mr. Speaker,
I do not want to belabour the House, I just want to make a few comments on the use of the word "strategy". This word is in common usage by members of the New Democratic Party in calling for a national industrial strategy and in calling for, as the present amendment provides, a Canadian marine industrial strategy. I would like to remind the House that the term "strategy" has to do with the things that are done in the tents of generals. It has not to do with the orderly laying out of a long-range plan which identifies goals, alternative means to reach those goals and the financial and physical wherewithal in order to carry out the pursuit of those objectives.
I am trying to submit that the use of the term "industrial strategy", which many have come to regard as a buzzword because the term appears in every speech made by the New Democratic Party, really creates a picture of conspiring behind closed doors and adapting strategy or plan of attack in order to take the best advantage of your opponent or competitor.
If that is what the NDP is trying to urge by its constant reference to the development of an industrial strategy, then its members are aiding and abetting the government which with every change of cabinet and with every change of economic conditions is creating new strategies. Often they are failed strategies, as we have seen by recent budgets.
What I am about to suggest to the NDP is that its members consider using a term that evokes a positive notion about what we are trying to achieve. In this present amendment, the wording could have been "Canadian marine development
19684

July 26, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
plan" rather than an "industrial strategy". We might get much further with that wording because we could then talk about an open public dialogue, with the co-operation of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) and the government, as to what the ingredients and essential elements of that plan might be. We could deal with issues like the recent decision of Dome Petroleum to build an LNG plant near Prince Rupert and trade off deals with the Japanese and others that that would entail. We could talk about whether or not in letting contracts for the development of the new port at Ridley Island we would award contracts for piling pipe to a Japanese company, for the car dumpers to a British company or for the stacker reclaimer equipment to another Japanese company. Both in this House and in committee we could debate the essential ingredients for an industrial development plan and stop playing games and talking about strategizing.
We have heard the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), ever since he was part of a conspiracy group that brought down the former Conservative government, talk about bringing in an industrial development strategy for Canada, but all we have seen is this document put out with the November 12 budget called "Economic Development for the Eighties". We have no specific delineation of objectives, targets and goals. We have not seen a critical and structural analysis of the alternative paths to achieving those goals, or a recommendation as to which would be the favourite path, how those goals could be achieved in terms of financial resources and in terms of the joint role of the private and public sector in pursuing those goals.
I am saying though that we should have a Canadian industrial plan and we should have a marine industrial plan which encompasses the ingredients of port policy. But for the life of me I cannot see how the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) feels that he can goad the government into developing this elusive Canadian industrial strategy by writing it into a piece of legislation. It has to be the consequence of sustained political pressure in this House both in question period and in committee. It will not achieve anything in terms of the goals which the hon. member is seeking by merely writing the words into a piece of legislation.
If the hon. member for Comox-Powell River reads subclauses (a) through (e) of Section 2(3), he will find that they do express the objectives of the national ports policy. We find these subclauses read:
(a)	is an effective instrument of support for the achievement of Canadian international trade objectives and of national, regional and local economic and social objectives;
(b)	is efficient;
(c)	provides accessibility and equitable treatment in the movement of goods and persons to users of Canadian ports;
(d)	provides local port corporations with a high degree of autonomy-
Some of the elements of an industrial plan for marine development are already there, and merely adding the words of his motion at the end of the subclause does not add anything of substance to Bill C-92 as presently presented.
If we had a Canadian marine industrial development plan within the context of a larger Canadian industrial development plan, then we would not have to deal with such a situation as the immature tactics of the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Lumley) have created by frustrating the import of Japanese automobiles. We would have long ago negotiated a Canada-Japan trade agreement parallel to the Canada-U.S. auto pact. We would not be playing these childish games with our very important trading partners in Japan and other Pacific countries. We would not have had to bring the Minister of Transport to a dead halt a year ago when he and his officials were dead-set to award contracts for the dredging at Roberts Bank to offshore, foreign firms when, in the final analysis, there was a reputable Canadian dredging company which won the bid after sustained representation by some members of British Columbia before the transport committee.
If we had a Canadian marine industrial development plan we would not have had the situation in 1974 or 1975 when representatives of the NDP government in British Columbia, with which the hon. member for Comox-Powell River enjoys some relationship, went to Stockholm, Sweden to buy a ferry because that government did not have the foresight to provide assistance to the west coast shipbuilding industry to build a ferry in British Columbia. We have hypocritical members in the New Democratic Party talking about Canada first and about an industrial development strategy favouring our shipbuilding industry, but their own friends in British Columbia went to Stockholm, Sweden to buy a large ferry which could have been manufactured in British Columbia using British Columbia labour.
We have had enough of this nonsense of people talking about strategy. Strategizing is exactly what we have been getting for far too long from the government opposite. Everything is done behind closed doors like a coterie of generals in their tents trying to decide how to stand off the enemy hordes. We should start planning out front with the public. We should take a logical and realistic approach to our trade relations with other countries, to our taxation policies, to our Canada first initiatives. We should do that in the context of an open public discussion through a standing committee, together with all Canadians across the country.
I suggest the words of the motion are wrong. The intent is admirable and commendable but the use of the term "strategy" is dead wrong.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I notice in the dictionary that the words "strategy" and "plan" mean the same thing. Might I have unanimous consent to change my motion, if it will remove the commi-pinko connotation of the word "strategy" and thus make my motion appealing to the Conservatives, by using the word "plan" in its place?
Yes, I will agree with that.
No.

Mr. Speaker, I will not take much time in the House to speak on this bill, but coming from the city of Victoria I should point out to the House how people feel about this bill.
First, 1 might say that we are quite concerned about the power that is going to flow to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) after this bill is passed. He has sufficient powers at the present time and to add to them seems to us unnecessary.
The port of Victoria being a public port, it will under the bill be entitled to a public harbour advisory committee whose role it will be to advise the minister. When the bill was published 1 wrote and asked the minister about this. Victoria does not have an ordinary harbour. Its harbour is scenic. Victoria's inner harbour is undergoing a lengthy and expensive process of removing a tank farm from the harbour shore. We did that solely because it was unsightly and we did not wish to have it in our harbour. When I think of what we might get in the way of a ministerially-appointed advisory committee, I would worry about it as much as the people around Peggy's Cove would worry if they found out that they were to have a refinery built there or were to start offloading LNG.
However, we have moved, by constant watchfulness of our own interests in Victoria, toward continued beautification of the harbour. For instance, it now has a walkaway around the entire inner harbour on the city side. As I say, this is not an ordinary kind of harbour. The rules made for Vancouver harbour or for Montreal harbour would not apply in Victoria at all. This is of great concern to us. For instance, they wanted to move the coast guard buildings to bring them together on the inner harbour or partly on the outer harbour, I suppose it was. The structure which they planned for that function was simply not acceptable to the people of Victoria. There was so much public outcry against it that the department had to look at it again and eventually come in, with a set of buildings which were acceptable. This is the kind of public participation in port planning which the city of Victoria wants. We know what we want there, but it seems to us that no one else seems to know.
In line with that, I wrote to the minister on March 25. I ended up by writing:
Your co-operation in ensuring a high level of municipal involvement would be appreciated.
I put that in after I had expressed my concern about the people who would be appointed to the harbour advisory committee.
The answer I received from the minister was not the one I had hoped for, by any means. I would respectfully submit that it may well have been part of a form letter which went to other members with harbours in their constituencies. He wrote:
Public harbour advisory councils will be made of three to five members, representative of local interests, and selected on the basis of their experience and capacity in port activities. The members shall be appointed by the Minister of Transport, to whom the council will provide its recommendations. Before appointing members, the advice of community leaders and port officials will be sought to ensure an effective council.
We have not had that kind of seeking out of advice from community leaders in Victoria. As far as I know to date, there
Canada Ports Corporation Act
has been a trip made to Victoria by some officials of the department, but we must have a continuing dialogue between the department and officials in Victoria, that is the municipal council, and the council of Esquimalt. It would be quite likely to cause a great deal of harm if the minister were to appoint people who were not in sympathy with the aims of the city fathers of the city of Victoria and the other municipalities involved.
I had hoped the minister would realize this, carry on negotiations out there and give us some intimation of who he was planning to appoint. If it is to be a bunch of Liberal hacks left over from some of the 78 constituencies which they lost in the west in the last election, then we would be better off without them. speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
