Mr. Speaker, I want to speak for a few moments in connection with the port and harbour of St. John's Newfoundland, while we are considering this bill. First of all, I want to point out that St. John's is one of the ports which comes under the old legislation that is being replaced by the present legislation. There are 14 ports, of which St. John's, Newfoundland, is one. Presumably St. John's, Newfoundland will be expected to become a local ports corporation at some future date if the legislation which we are considering now is passed by the House.
Also I want to point out to the minister that the port of St. John's, Newfoundland, which is a major port in that capital city, has had no major capital expenditures in connection with that facility since 1965. Of course, the expenditures in 1965 were a result of a program commenced by the Diefenbaker administration to improve the harbour facilities in St. John's. If we look at St. John's and then look at other ports in Canada, by comparison huge sums have been spent in these other ports. I am not saying that the spending on these other ports is improper or not needed, but just let me point out that in the port of Saint John, New Brunswick, for example, over the period of the last ten years at least S80 to $90 million has been spent on capital projects.
I could look at all kinds of other ports across the country where I could point to tens and tens of millions of dollars being spent. I could point out the unfairness of what happened with respect to the synchrolift facility in the dockyard of St. John's, Newfoundland where the federal Government of Canada, which owns the dockyard, would not spend $21 million to instal a synchrolift that would make the dockyard viable, a dockyard which it was given free, gratis, in 1949. At the same time it spent double that amount in Halifax to assist in its new shipyard facilities and, of course, the same occurred in Vancouver and other ports. I will skip all that, but the harbour facilities in St. John's have not been improved since 1965.
There was an order in council on January 15, 1981 under which the government assumed responsibility for the long-term debt of the National Harbours Board. I believe it was about

July 26, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
$300 million, but the government assumed responsibility for that debt. It relieved the National Harbours Board of interest charges of something like $18.4 million as a result of taking over the debt. Those interest charges and that debt were incurred in other major ports which now have major capital improvements but are debt free.
The result of this action by the government was that these ports are debt free. They had major capital costs which they no longer have. There was no assistance to ports such as St. John's, Newfoundland, that did not have any capital expenditure debt which could be written off at that particular time. The port of St. John's has an operating deficit of about $2 million.
I want to ask the minister whether it is the plan to have the government assume the debts of ports such as St. John's which were not included or received no benefit from the assumption of the debt by order in council on January 15, 1981. For example, what is to happen to the debt of the port of St. John's Newfoundland?
Also I want to ask the minister whether it is the intention to have the port of St. John's, Newfoundland, become a local ports corporation. The legislation suggests that a port cannot become a local ports corporation unless it is found to be financially viable. As I understand it, at the present time the port of St. John's, Newfoundland with the facilities which it now has is not financially viable. Therefore, what is to happen? Is that port to be left in limbo and run directly from Ottawa, from the headquarters of the new ports corporation with its local advisory board, or will it be given the right to a local management and some assistance to obtain the facilities which will enable it to become financially self-supporting?
When the minister has a chance, I would like him to enlighten me on that particular area. The whole justification for this new act is that it will allow for decentralized authority, local port management and operation, rather than the highly centralized control under the present act. For example, St. John's has a purely advisory body at the moment. I think it is called the St. John's port authority board. It is purely advisory.
I do not think there is any statutory authority for their offices. Mr. Robert Innes is the chairman of that advisory body, but as far as I know there is no legal basis for his position at all. In any event, they only advise central headquarters. The other members are Mr. Humphries, regional director of the Canadian Coast Guard, Newfoundland region; Michael Walsh, general chairman of the Brotherhood and Railway Clerks Union-there are political appointments-Gerald Tilley, general manager of Carling O'Keefe Breweries of Canada Ltd.; and two others who are well-known Liberals. That does not mean to say that they do not have a contribution to make, but William Callahan was a former Liberal member of the House of Assembly and cabinet minister, and Mr. George Stockley was certainly a Liberal supporter in the past. Mr. Innes himself was a Liberal candidate in my byelection of 1976. God, how long have 1 been here? It has been too long!
Hear, hear!

Mr. Innes ran against me in the byelection of October 18, 1976, but I was returned on that occasion. It was the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) birthday. I was glad to be the birthday present they returned from St. John's West. I hope to be here when we finally give him the coup de grace when the next election comes.
In any event, Bob Innes was a Liberal candidate. That is not to say that he is not a fine gentleman and not doing a good job, because as far as I know, he is. Even a Liberal can have some virtue. There are some around who have something to be said for them. I do not know what has happened to me today! The spirit of kindliness and consideration has just swept over me. We have been here too long; it is time for this place to adjourn.
In any event, it is an illustration of the weakness of this system that patronage is so much a part of it. Of this six-man advisory council, at least three are certainly publicly identified Liberals, two are ex-candidates and, unfortunately, that does not give the right tone to such an important body. The port of St. John's harbour is very important to our whole economy, and to have the public feel that you must be a Liberal to be appointed to this advisory board and that is the only way you will get there unless we obtain power in the next election- when we do, we will certainly reverse that and put in the merit system. You will have to be a Conservative to merit any appointment then.
But that is a weakness of this system. I would prefer a system where certain bodies have to nominate representatives-and I think this is included in one of the amendments we are coming to-where at least half of the members would be nominated from various users of the port facilities, and the municipality. As I said, I have nothing against these gentlemen and they are doing their best against very high odds.
I also want to suggest to the minister that it is essential when this legislation is passed that the minor ports of Canada, of which St. John's is one in the context of Vancouver, and giant ports like Halifax and Toronto, have representatives on the national board of directors of this new corporation that we are setting up.
It is my understanding that of the 11 directors who will be on the board of this new corporation, three will be port authority chairmen. If this is the case and if I have my facts correct, then I suggest to the minister that he should make sure that these chairmen do not just come from Montreal, Vancouver and Halifax or from the three largest ports, and that, if at all possible, we have at least one from every province. There certainly should be a representative from Newfoundland-I suggest from the Port of St. John's-on the new board of directors of this authority. We have a Newfoundland representative on the board of Air Canada, another good Liberal. He raised funds and did his best to have me defeated in the 1976 byelection. I will do my best to see that he is transferred from Air Canada when we take our rightful place in office. But we do have a representative on the board of Air Canada
July 26, 1982

and a representative on the board of the CNR, and therefore I suggest that it is very important-even more important-for us to have a representative of the province on the new Canada Ports Corporation.
Another point I wanted to make to the minister is that all of the transportation spending in Newfoundland in the last few years has been on modes other than the port of St. John's, which badly needs new facilities. St. John's has been trying to get new container facilities since 1976. It has been seeking $19.6 million, the cost some years ago of contructing the container facilities that are needed, which was turned down by the Treasury Board after my election in the byelection of 1976.
1 do not know if there is any connection between those two events. In any event, St. John's has been trying since then to obtain funding for this very necessary facility and there has not been any funding.
As the minister knows, there has been a major revitalization program for the railway; I believe it is $77 million. The harbour needs funds as well or it will fall into disuse. The minister has also announced spending of $70 million; $48 million for highways and $20 million for new airstrips on the Labrador coast. All this is necessary but 1 want to point out to him that it is necessary to spend some money on the port of St. John's, particularly now with the new set-up that is envisaged in this legislation.
I know that we do not have too much time, but while speaking about St. John's, it is extremely important that a freezer facility be constructed at the west end finger pier that would enable the transshipment of fish which are unloaded from one vessel to be stored in the freezer facility and then transferred to another vessel for shipment. This would give the longshoremen at St. John's very badly needed employment. This freezer facility would also enable ships to store cargo when they had to go on the synchrolift to be repaired. This freezer facility is an important issue in St. John's. I hope the minister or this new corporation will see that the necessary steps are taken.
One final point 1 would like to make while talking about the port of St. John's is that we have 276 registered fishermen in the port of St. John's. Anyone who travels through the narrows, as we call them, through that majestic entrance into St. John's harbour, with Cabot Tower located on Signal Hill and where the first telegraph message was sent across the Atlantic by Marconi at the beginning of the century, will see as they look down below at The Battery the residences of a number of fishermen perched on the rocks of The Battery. When one looks at the other side of the port in the district of St. John's West, Fort Amherst, one will see the homes of other fishermen who are constituents of mine. St. John's is also a fishing port. It is not just a port but a fishing port where we have a major fish plant of National Sea Products Limited. Of course, it is supplied largely by trawlers but they also take inshore fish. There are also other smaller fishing operations in that port.
These fishermen are, at the moment, dispossessed. They do not have any proper facilities in the port of St. John's for landing their fish, and the place where they formerly landed their fish is now being dredged and construction has begun for
Canada Ports Corporation Act
the new synchrolift. These fishermen do not have proper landing facilities, haul-out equipment and storage facilities, all of which they badly need.
There is now a plan by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans to construct a facility at Prosser's Rock, but that even will take two or three years. It will be some time before it comes, a three-year period starting in 1983-84, we are told. The cost will be $4 million to $7 million for wharves and fish landing facilities. In the meantime we have 100 boats, 157 fishermen, 12.5 million pounds of fish that were caught last year from the port of St. John's which has a landed value of $2.5 million. We have workers there who are operating the two fish plants. The facilities for fishermen are badly needed.
We did propose a breakwater and facilities at The Battery but unfortunately the government, when it took over in 1980, stopped the plan that would see this carried out.
We have a number of users in the port of St. John's who have to be looked after. The fishermen are the most neglected of all of those users. 1 would like the minister, or the new port corporation, to see what they can do to help the Department of Fisheries and Oceans obtain some funds to instal proper facilities for these several hundred Newfoundland fishermen who are so important to the local economy.
Those are my remarks with reference to the port of St. John's. I would like to turn to another subject when we come to a relevant amendment, or to third reading, which I think is of great gravity and importance. It concerns a most deplorable situation in the port of Goose Bay, Labrador. It cannot be allowed to go any further without complete public ventilation.
I am not satisfied at all with any steps which the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) has taken to rectify a situation of gouging the consumers of the Happy Valley-Labrador area of Newfoundland. I will expand on this subject at my next opportunity. If the minister can give me any information on these points, I would appreciate it.

Mr. Speaker, most of the answers my hon. friend asks for are in the committee proceeding. Indeed, St. John's did not have many debts to be forgiven and consequently did not benefit as much as others did. A certain amount of debt was kept in the books for most of the ports, if not all. With respect to St. John's, it is $1.7 million but in Saint John, New Brunswick, it is $7.2 million. Montreal is $9,470 million, which gives some indication of the principle that was implemented in this situation.
I just want to emphasize the fact that should the port of St. John's ever have needs greater than its financial self-sufficiency can take, all ports, including St. John's, will be entitled to grants from the Canadian government. So, the concept of selfsufficiency, which is an important one, does not mean that if the needs are beyond the financial capacity of the ports for particular projects, the Government of Canada will stay idle.
With regard to the local port corporation, my information is that St. John's is eligible to become one. With regard to the composition of the Canada Ports Corporation, it will be

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Following the decision made earlier this day by the Speaker, motions Nos. 2 and 4 are to be grouped for debate. The Speaker ruled that because both motions are concerned with the principle of financial selfsufficiency, a vote on motion No. 2 would dispose of motion No. 4. Accordingly, I will also put motion No. 4 at this time, for purposes of debate.

Motion No. 4
That Bill C-92, An Act to amend the National Harbours Board Act, the Government Harbours and Piers Act, the Harbour Commissions Act, the Canada Shipping Act and the Fishing and Recreational Harbours Act, be amended in Clause 5 by striking out lines 8 and 9 at page 11.
She said: Mr. Speaker, the subject of these amendments is economic, financial self-sufficiency in the case of local port corporations, better known as the Liberal policy of "user-pay" which, of course, is a policy which is fully supported by the Conservatives to my right. We are very concerned about these two clauses. I would just like to read for the record how Clause
2, under the objectives of the new port legislation, would read if amended as we propose:
(2) It is further declared that achievement of the objective of the national ports policy requires
(a) the establishment at ports of national or regional significance at which
there is demonstrated local interest in the management thereof and that are
expected to be financially self-sufficient-
That is the part of the bill with which we are concerned. We are fully in favour of local autonomy for as many ports in Canada as possible. We really do not agree that the whole criterion of financial self-sufficiency should be a prohibition to ports having a decentralized form of administration, having power within the regions to make their own decisions to the greatest possible degree and having their own board which is hopefully representative of the various levels of the region, the local levels of government and so on.
We are also concerned with the rather insidious wording of this clause. I wonder what is meant by "ports that are expected to be financially self-sufficient". Just what does that mean? If we take a look at the 15 ports which are listed as ports which may be eligible to become local port corporations, we find that quite a few of them have not been economically and financially self-sufficient in the past. For the record, I would like to list those 15 ports.
We heard about St. John's, Newfoundland from the hon. member who spoke quite eloquently. I am sure he knows it is not likely to be always financially self-sufficient, yet why should it not have local autonomy under good administrative practices, even if it occasionally does need some form of federal subsidy?
Halifax, Nova Scotia, is another port which I do not believe has been traditionally self-sufficient.
Then there is the port at Saint John, New Brunswick. In committee we heard of the great concern of one of the members, which we would share, that although the federal government has written off the debts of most ports, there is still a considerable debt in that case, and although it came through the province, there should certainly be fair treatment of that port. If it wants to become a local port corporation in the future, why should it not have that right, even if it may require some subsidization at some future time?
Belledune, New Brunswick, is another port. There are also Sept-Iles and Chicoutimi in Quebec. I do not believe those three ports have always been financially self-sufficient in the past. Baie des Ha! Ha! in Quebec has shown a profit, as has Trois Rivieres. These two ports have shown a profit and would probably qualify under this specific criterion. The port at Quebec City has not shown a profit, nor has the port at Montreal, which are both very important ports.
Prescott elevator, which handles mostly grain, has shown a profit, and so has Colborne elevator in Ontario, another grain elevator. So those are two which have some source of income.
The port of Churchill, Manitoba is one of the best examples of a very essential port, both from a regional and a national
July 26, 1982

point of view. It operates only part of the year, due to its location, but should certainly have the right to be a real port corporation with local autonomy, under its own local board, even though we know that it will probably not always continue to be financially self-sufficient.
The port of Vancouver is also financially self-sufficient. It has not found that it has had very much power over the funds it has taken in. It has not been ale to reinvest the funds into the kinds of development that are very much needed to upgrade the port, and it has only been allowed up to $50,000 in expenditures, which is not even enough for the improvement of wharfs. However, that port does show a surplus and would be eligible under this legislation, I assume.
In the past Prince Rupert has not always shown a surplus, nor has it always been financially independent. There have been many new developments in Prince Rupert which will undoubtedly increase its income and make it a part of the major development in the northern part of British Columbia.
I wanted to name those 15 ports for the record to show that this legislation is really very unfair. Will ports which cannot become financially self-sufficient be able to qualify under this legislation? We have heard that these 15 ports may be candidates for local port corporations. Of course, we know that one of the reasons at this time which may make them eligible is that the accumulated debt of all 15 national ports was written off by the federal government in 1980. It was approved by order in council on January 15, 1981. This accumulated debt was $742 million. Approximately $500 million went toward principal and $242 million went toward interest.
That is why we are pleased to hear at this particular time that the ports of Canada are in very good condition. It was a very good move to write off outstanding debts so they could have a fresh start as autonomous ports. But what will happen, as shown by our past history? While all 15 ports made a profit last year because of this write-off, it should be pointed out that 10 of the 15 ports ran up deficits over the last two years. This is an indication that these ports will face financial difficulty in the next decade. They cannot be expected to be financially independent all the time. The only ports which did not run a deficit over the two years were Baie des Ha! Ha!, Trois Rivieres, Prescott elevator, Col borne elevator and Vancouver, not very many of the 15 ports. This does not even include the larger ports. Some ports may start off in the black. In a particularly bad year or bad economic era, they may end up with a deficit and require a subsidy from the federal government. Would they lose their status as local port corporations or not be judged reliable enough to get in in the first place?
We object to this policy because it is the user-pay policy. My colleague will speak to this later. The principle of user-pay, in other words financial self-sufficiency, means that ports should be able to finance their operations totally from collected fees and tariffs. This would include any capital expenditures that may be required. 1 am most familiar with the port of Vancouver. However, most ports require modernization and updating
Canada Ports Corporation Act
with modern equipment in order to be competitive with each other and the American ports. This will require capital expenditures. A port which must borrow in order to expand will have to pay market interest rates on loans. This could force a port to increase its charges to a level where it is no longer competitive, forcing an undue hardship on any shipper using the port.
The port of Churchill is a good example. How could that port be expected to make up any deficit of its operational cost over income by charging higher rates to users of that port? We must have a port in northern Canada, an outlet to our northern waters. The few users of that northern port should not be expected to bear the additional financial costs of its being in the Arctic region.
Our ports must remain competitive and continue to serve the national interest as well as the interest of our exporters and importers. In order to do this, they should be eligible for some form of federal assistance when it is required. This should be carried out under a strict business arrangement. We fully agree that the port must have efficient and competent management.
If the federal government is putting extra money into a port, perhaps there could be some form of federal supervision. However, that port should not lose all power. In fact, the goal of this bill, which is to make the ports more efficient, would be undermined if we removed the local administration of a port. They cannot be treated like a child and told that they have to come back to big daddy in Ottawa to be looked after, even though there are all kinds of bureaucratic roadblocks, it would cost more money and does not add to efficiency.
Clause 2(a) requires that ports be financially self-sufficient. If this is a required objective, ten of the 15 national ports may not qualify to become local port corporations. The same can hold true of our amendment which is on page 11 and combined in this amendment. It states that the Canada ports corporation can petition for local port corporation status for any port which in the opinion of the Canada Ports Corporation will likely be self-sufficient.
It is not likely over the long term that many ports will be self-sufficient. Does that mean those ports cannot become local port corporations? I am going to be very interested in hearing the Conservative members speak to this. Those members, particularly those from the Vancouver area, have been very quiet about the needs of the less affluent ports in Canada. Those of us from Vancouver fight hard for more financial autonomy for Vancouver. As Members of Parliament we must be equally concerned with a national transportation and marine strategy for ports in other parts of the country.
Smaller ports with limited revenues will not always be able to raise the amount they need to cover their costs through tariffs and fees. If they did that, they would likely lose business. They would have to charge too much. It would not be financially feasible from the customer's point of view. Those ports would find it hard to survive. We need efficient management based on sound regional considerations and a sound

July 26, 1982
Adjournment Motion
national policy for each local port. Efficient management should be the criterion for a port becoming more administratively autonomous.
Efficiency requires a centralized administration. This is best suited to the regional situation. The National Harbours Board has not worked effectively because most decisions were made in Ottawa. Who in Ottawa really knows the immediate needs of ports on our east and west coasts? Rather than central control, there should be local autonomy for the ports, even those not financially independent. However, the federal government should be very concerned about the efficient management of those ports once they become local port corporations.
We object to the term "financial self-sufficiency", which is a requirement for a port to become a local port corporation. This whole bill is supposedly aimed at greater autonomy. It is contradictory. Only four or five ports will be eligible to remain as local port corporations. Also, those ports that have more expenditures than income must not increase their fees and tariffs to the point that it is a user-pay philosophy that is unrealistic. Where the market can accept it, the users should pay. However, that is not the case with all ports in Canada.
That objective is not feasible for certain smaller ports in Canada. We believe the criterion for achieving local port autonomy should be demonstrated efficiency. A port which is essential to the regional and national economy should be eligible for local port corporation status, even if it cannot always be financially self-sufficient. It should not be forced to raise rates beyond what is financially feasible for the region.
I will be very interested to hear from the other parties. We did not have support or consensus in committee on this matter. In a country as large and diverse as Canada and in the context of a national ports policy, it is essential that we be very concerned about smaller ports which cannot always be financially self-sufficient.

Mr. Speaker, I will try to be somewhat more gentle than my colleague. In

July 26, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
looking at the two amendments proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs Mitchell), motions Nos. 2 and 4, 1 note that motion No. 2 would strike from page 3 of the bill the phrase "and that are expected to be financially self-sufficient" and subsequently that Motion No. 4 would delete the phrase on page 11 of the bill "the port will likely be financially selfsufficient".
Once again the NDP is getting into a great panic about something of little consequence. The wording in the bill does not say that a local port operating as a local port corporation "shall be self-sufficient". Neither on page 3 nor on page 11 does the bill say a local port "shall be". It does not say anywhere in the bill that local ports which run in the red "shall be closed down" or "shall be expected to earn profits or balance their books". It does not say that anywhere. All it says in the bill is that ports will likely be financially self-sufficient or that ports are expected to be financially self-sufficient.
The point is that we have to provide some goals for the local port corporations to pursue. I am sure that the minister and members of the government would agree with that. We are at a time in our history when we have almost $120 billion in gross public debt, $20 billion of additional debt this year and a $17 billion cash requirement which the government supplements by dipping into the pension fund of public service employees for the extra $2 or $3 billion. We are facing a horrendous situation where young people cannot afford mortgages for homes, where businesses are going bankrupt and our industries cannot compete internationally. We have been living too long in a dream world, believing that we could socialize, nationalize and subsidize everything that cannot operate by itself.
If we could restore a degree of local autonomy to the financial management and long-range planning of our ports, they would become more productive. There would be less interference by layers of bureaucracy in Ottawa and the layer that this legislation envisages. If the ports were given a higher degree of local autonomy, they could get on with making decisions, making long-range plans, making investments without being delayed by a lot of the factors that are initiated supposedly in the national interest, but which in fact pull the country down. If our ports were in a more healthy state of competition one with the other, the would produce more volume and more tax revenue to be shared by all Canadians. I think it is high time we recognized that.
The situation is rather like that of a class of 20 students where, instead of the incentive system operating where they would be urged to generate grades in proportion to their ability and effort, at the end of the year the marks of the individual students would be combined and then averaged. Each student would obtain the same average mark, so the achiever who would otherwise have obtained a 85 or 90 per cent grade would receive 64.5 per cent and the sluggard who would have received 48 or 28 per cent, would also get 64.5 per cent. Pretty soon there would be a demoralized class of low achievers or non-achievers.
That is what we are producing in this country. By distributing the benefits, so-called, of effort equally among all, we destroy the basic incentive system that allows our society to prosper and grow.
I submit that if you followed the students in that class of 20 for two or three years, you would find that the average would slip from 64 per cent to 54 per cent to 48 per cent. Pretty soon it would be a failing class and would require a subsidy. Teachers who find that the class average is lower than 50 per cent-I have been a teacher and I know-would say that the incentive system had been destroyed so the marks should be augmented and all pushed above 50 per cent.
That is an exact analogy to the kind of subsidies our colleagues on the left are forever advocating and which destroy the spirit of this country, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) is one of the worst offenders. In committee he showed righteous indignation, wailing and raving that if we asked the ports to be self-sufficient, that was an evil thing. He well knows that our young people cannot find jobs or afford homes today because we are borrowing too heavily. He knows that the CBC is subsidized to the tune of $650 million per year, that Air Canada got a $500 to $600 million transfusion three years ago and now Claude Taylor says they will need another one within a year. The CNR has come back to committee looking for another major subsidy and Petro-Canada is continually dipping into the Canadian taxpayer's pocket to subsidize the so-called initiative that was designed to pursue the national objectives of equity and fairness.
In fact, what we are doing is what the teacher would do to that class of achievers, and that is destroying the desire to achieve. Sooner or later it will be a class of failing students which will have to be subsidized by jacking the marks up so that they can obtain a passable grade. The achiever would be dispirited, and the sluggard would ask why bother as they will pass anyway.
That is exactly the situation in this country today. We are destroying the basic competitive, incentive system. I submit that the present wording of the bill before us incorporates that competitive opportunity for individual ports by encouraging them to operate on a self-sufficient basis. We are not heartless or cold and ruthless in this party. There is no one here who would say we are not in favour of helping where such help would be of benefit to the national interest. But we have seen too much of the slovenly, wasteful extravagance of an ever-diminishing pool of revenue which is only the measure of the over-all effort of individuals operating in a free society. That must be brought to a halt.
I commend the minister for including these clauses in the bill and I am totally against the suggestion that we should put all our national ports on the welfare rolls, as we have put so many Canadians on the welfare rolls.

Mr. Speaker, it is difficult to reply to the hon. member except to suggest that if
July 26, 1982

he wants a first rate example of vacuous remarks he should read his own speech tomorrow.
The hon. gentleman and the member who preceded him have not looked at the realities of operating transportation facilities in this country. In the history of the country they have never been self-sufficient nor will they become selfsufficient in the long term.
My colleague the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) mentioned the write-offs of debts. Back in 1936, $173 million was written off for local port authorities.
That was a great year.

Yes, the Tories had just finished being in power. In 1977-78 they wrote off another $252 million which was put into equity ownership by the Government of Canada, and a further $475 million was converted to an interest-free loan. Halifax had $54 million written off, Saint John $66 million, Chicoutimi $8.4 million, Quebec $104 million. Three Rivers $4 million-all those were total write-offs, transferred to equity. Interest free loans totalled $475 million, $100 million of which is owed by the port of Vancouver. I do not think any government that was in power would ever call in those debts; if it did, the port of Vancouver would go belly up the next month.
Like other transportation sectors, ports are capital intensive sectors of the economy; they require massive amounts of capital. To follow the user-pay principle to its logical conclusion, you would need cost recovery just to break even. I suspect what would happen is what happened before-the smaller ports would go broke and the bigger ports would run into rate wars with ports in the United States. Then they would be the first to run to the federal government asking to be bailed out, as has happened repeatedly over the decades.
A port, like a street, a sidewalk, a sewer and water system or highway, is a facility that everyone has to use, directly or indirectly; it is a public utility. If user-pay were followed to its logical conclusion, toll booths would be put up every four or five blocks and pedestrians would be charged two bits for walking on the sidewalk. Pedestrians do not pay anything toward the cement; the people who own the property on the street pay taxes. Followed to its logical conclusion you see how ridiculous it is. You can go back to the feudal ages of toll roads where the kings and dukes and the lords charged the peasants to walk, ride a horse or haul their produce down a road which belonged to the king or the lord.
These kings, dukes and lords over here see things like they did in the middle ages: if the port of Churchill cannot break even or make a profit, close it down. I hope the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook) is invited to speak to the Churchill chamber of commerce, because I would like him to tell that to them. We will not have to bother, although we are going to tell them anyway.
In a country, Mr. Speaker, of three million square miles and only 25 million people, these birds over here want to compete
Canada Ports Corporation Act
in a champagne league with a beer operation. There is no way that individual ports, totally autonomous and on their own, can compete with the ports of our neighbour to the south. If you think the U.S. government is going to hold still for any kind of rate cutting or anything like that in Vancouver, you are dreaming in technicolour. If the government thinks that ports on the eastern seaboard of the United States are going to hold still while Halifax, St. John's and Montreal are siphoning off business from them, again it is dreaming. Part of co-operative federalism is that we share in a reasonable and equitable way the cost of providing services which all of us depend on directly and indirectly. That is more true of transportation than almost any other sector of our economy.
For those reasons, running our ports with a so-called businesslike user-pay policy will not succeed. I hope I turn out to be wrong, but I never thought I would live to see the day when Tories would support the user-pay policy of Otto Lang. I did not think the present minister would subscribe to it but he obviously is.
In converting all these debts, Mr. Speaker, we are now hopefully starting off most, if not all, of these ports with a clean slate. There are still some things wrong, and I sympathize a bit with the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), a port which I do not think was treated fairly in the debt rearrangement. That port has to pay interest on 86 per cent of its long-term debt structure compared to 4 per cent for Montreal and zero for Quebec and Vancouver. I hope the hon. member will talk to his friends in North Vancouver-Burnaby about that one.
Let us consider, Mr. Speaker, the unfortunate remarks of the hon. member about Churchill. It is funny that countries with less resources than we have, financial or economic, are able to operate Arctic ports for six to nine months of the year. I am thinking of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia, and even some of the ports in the northern islands of Japan. Churchill should be able to operate six or seven months of the year and then it might become a break-even operation. It might even make a buck the odd year. That requires a large capital investment, but the benefits of that investment mean lower grain and potash shipping costs and higher exports through that port will repay the investment. The question is, should that cost be paid only by our export customers? Because if it is, they are not going to buy from us. When the cost of transportation goes up for those kinds of products, you cannot pass it on to your customers. We found that out from bitter experience in the grain trade. But out of the port of Churchill the shipping rates are lower. We get hit in the head sometimes on marine insurance rates, but that port could be and should be at least a six or seven-month-a-year operation.
Just because we buried the old debts, Mr. Speaker, and thereby gave the federal government that much equity in the ports does not mean we can apply user-pay in the future, because ports are so capital intensive. They will be required to be competitive with U.S. ports. Our ports earned only a 2.5 per

July 26, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
cent return in 1980, and it is perfectly obvious they will not be able to raise enough capital in the future or they will lose money trying to pay the interest even if interest rates go down. Therefore the requirement in the bill that port corporations be totally self-sufficient is completely unrealistic. It has never worked before and it will not work in the future.
I would like someone to give me a list of ports around the world which are self-sufficient and have had no public investment or government subsidies. 1 do not care whether it is New York City, Seattle, San Francisco, New Orleans, Galveston or wherever, they have all been heavily subsidized, and you cannot expect one port in Canada to compete with the treasury of the United States or any other country. It will not work and it never has. As I said before, I hope I turn out to be wrong.
This bill is some kind of a compromise. I appreciate that it is an attempt by the government to come up somewhere between complete local autonomy and total government control of the operation. That is what the government is endeavouring to do. Typical of a Liberal government, because Liberals call themselves middle of the road, but that is where all the accidents happen. I do not think it is going to work, and I predict it will not work.
If I am lucky enough to be honoured by my voters to be here four or five years down the road, I predict that whoever is in government will be coming to Parliament with some refinancing or interest-free loans for a number of ports in this country. It is inevitable. If my hon. friend from North Vancou-ver-Burnaby and my hon. friend from Richmond-South Delta think that Vancouver can, forever and a day, operate on its own, again they are dreaming in technicolour. In fact, if they are so good I presume the new local port authority for Vancouver will want to pay back the $100 million that it owes to the government. I presume they will rush forward with a cheque the next day.
Without public input on behalf of all the people of Canada, Mr. Speaker, the ports I have listed could never have survived let alone grow. That is the reality of transportation in this country, the reality of ports. I suppose I have to give the minister credit; it is an honest attempt to arrive at something in between what was done earlier and what is done now. I wish him well. I hope it succeeds, but I predict it will not.
You are a pessimist.

The bill does provide for something I presume the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby does not agree with. It provides an opportunity for cross-subsidization within the ports system. This was not possible under the existing National Harbours Board Act which requires special parliamentary approval for each individual port. The Canada Ports Corporation has access to surpluses of profitable ports with which to finance or assist in financing unprofitable ones.
In spite of what the two hon. gentlemen from Vancouver have said I do not think that the people in Vancouver or anyone connected with the Vancouver port want to run the
port of Prince Rupert into the ground. In spite of the actions of Liberal governments, I think the people in Montreal really do not want to starve and bankrupt the ports of Churchill, Saint John or Halifax. The nation as a whole has to share in the costs of operating efficient and well run ports with local authorities and with the total national backing in the interests of a whole nation. This must not be done in the interests of some local board of trade or in the interests of one shipper or user, but in the interests of the nation as a whole.
From the list of ports I have in front of me I cannot see any of them that are not in the national interest, whether it is Belledune, Sept-Iles, Prescott, Colbourne, Prince Rupert or Roberts Bank. They are all in the national interest. They all play an important role in the commerce of this nation. But none of them, and I include Vancouver and Montreal, can operate entirely on its own and say to hell with the rest of the country.
In the name of some kind of co-operative federalism-a name that used to be popular some years ago and should be revived-whether it is between governments, whether it is among ports or any other sectors of our economy, I have had enough of this. "Beggar thy neighbour; as long as we are doing all right, to hell with the other guy" is the kind of philosophy we have been getting from these gentlemen to my right and south of the 49th parallel.
User-pay cannot work. In a nation of three million square miles with only 24 million people and dozens of ports, it cannot work. To suggest that the people in a community of one or more different ports, whether it be Churchill or any other are to be told, presumably by a Conservative government, that their port is not making the bucks or breaking even and now they have to get up and walk away from it, throwing the taxpayer's investment out of the window as well as their own, is just not right. It is like a previous minister of transport and the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) abandoning branch lines and telling the farmers who own all the grain elevators that they are supposed to get up and walk away from their investment. User-pay does not work and it will not work.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Out of courtesey to the hon. member I did not want to interrupt his tirade at the time, but at least five times he got the name of my riding incorrectly. I would not want any other member in the immediate area to be confused with the hon. member to whom he was directing his tirade. The correct name of my riding is North Vancouver-Burnaby. If I can bootleg, I would be delighted to go to Churchill to speak to the chamber of commerce or the board of trade.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to point out to the people in the galleries that they have just witnessed a debate by the
July 26, 1982

Conservatives and by the New Democratic Party. I would now like to demonstrate a typical Liberal solution to this impasse.
I think what the hon. member from the New Democratic Party wants to achieve by her amendment is already in the bill. The purpose of the whole bill is to give a greater degree of autonomy to the National Elarbours Board system. The hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon) identified himself as a teacher. I do not know if I should be following him because my experience has been that of a school principal. However, he made very good arguments and he must have been an excellent teacher in his time. In my view, though, he was a little harsh in his interpretation of the bill.
I think he was correct when he said the hon. member proposes to remove in two places "expected to be financially self-sufficient". Specifically her amendment would remove these words from Clause 2, subclause 2(a). The bill clearly states that the local port corporations are only expected-I underline the word expected, not required-to be self-sufficient. There is this room for flexibility.
The bill contains numerous provisions for assistance, if needed. For example, the Canadian Ports Corporation may transfer money to the local port corporation. The Canadian Ports Corporation may loan money to the local port corporation, an excellent amendment which the committee brought into this bill. The local port corporation may borrow from the government or from outside if this local port corporation after maturing receives Schedule D status. The government may make grants to the local port corporation.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) in her speech asked whether the ports that cannot become financially self-sufficient will be eligible to qualify for local ports status. The answer clearly is yes, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member listed ten ports which may not qualify for the status, but that is not true; they all qualify. Maybe not immediately, but they all qualify when the people in the local community, the businessmen, the residents, the municipalities and the users demonstrate a genuine interest, a will, a commitment, and maybe some prognosis that eventually the port will become selfsufficient. There may be a need beyond the capacity to pay now, but the projection would have to show that the port could become self-sufficient. However, achieving local port corporation status is already in the bill. I think if the hon. member studies the bill carefully she may even want to withdraw her amendment.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
I am not sure whether you are Mr. Chairman or Mr. Speaker, but whatever you are I am obedient to your wishes. 1 see that you are Mr. Speaker. I wish to speak for just a couple of moments on the question of whether a port is self-supporting. I have no argument with my colleagues from Vancouver, British Columbia, as to the necessity, if at all possible, of having a port operate to make money, break even or whatever. But when we take a look at what ports are making money, breaking even, doing well or doing less well, then I would like to ensure that they are all being looked at on the same basis.
Canada Ports Corporation Act
1 can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that if the port of St. John's, Newfoundland had the same advantages given to it, the same kind of financial assistance and benefits that are given to the port of Quebec City, the port of Montreal, the port of Halifax or the port of Saint John, New Brunswick-I am not too familiar with the Port of Vancouver-then the port of St. John's, Newfoundland, would be making as much money as those ports, breaking even or whatever.
I am supportive of this bill on the understanding that ports such as St. John's, Newfoundland, which the accountants tell us are not making money, are not breaking even and have to be subsidized, will be treated fairly and put in a position where they can run their own affairs after being put on an equal basis with the other ports of Canada. At the present time, the port of St. John's, Newfoundland, has not been put in that position.
I can give, although I do not want to bore the House or delay the bill, a dozen instances where the port of St. John's, Newfoundland, has not been treated in a manner comparable to other places.
I remember looking at a press release issued by one of the government departments which told us that three or four cabinet ministers had been down to Quebec City and that tens of millions of dollars were going to be spent on the port of Quebec City restoring the old dockside, old sheds, or old warehouses. In other words, doing wonderful things for the historic trust kind of thing in the city of Quebec. I say that that is great and that I am all for it. I am glad this is being done for Quebec City, but I have not seen any cabinet ministers crawling around the port of St. John's, Newfoundland lashing out the tens of millions to restore the historic sites.
As a matter of fact, next year in St. John's we are having the four hundredth anniversary of the taking of possession of Newfoundland by Sir Humphrey Gilbert on behalf of the British Crown in 1583. It will be 400 years ago next year that the British empire had its commencement in the port of St. John's, Newfoundland. The war memorial is on Duckworth Street facing the harbour. A plan has been developed and there was a competition award. The plan which was approved was done by a young landscape architect from Newfoundland who was just back from university a year or two ago. This young chap, Fred Hann, has done a first-class job. He won this award for the celebrations next year, and now we have to spend certain moneys to develop a proper park. Sir Humphrey Gilbert Park, where Sir Humphrey originally took possession of Newfoundland and began the process which led to the British empire.
It is very hard for the committee to come by any funds. It is awaiting funds from the federal government. We are not talking about millions. We are talking about some hundreds of thousands; certainly not the tens of millions which were lashed into Quebec City. 1 am all for lashing it into Quebec City as long as it is lashed elsewhere. The committee is waiting to hear from the provincial government as well. The whole cost of the
Canada Ports Corporation Act
project-and 1 am going from memory now-is not much above $1 million or $1.5 million to put a proper park and memorial right on the St. John's waterfront in front of the war memorial.
We do not see any great enthusiasm from the government opposite. Perhaps it is because there are two Conservative members representing the city of St. John's, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and myself. We are going to be here for donkeys' years yet. They would not move us with a crowbar. It does not matter whether they starve the city of St. John's and refuse to spend money. Those people will send us back, and if we do not run they will send other Conservatives back. They will add another five in the next election anyway. Newfoundland will return 100 per cent Tories when the next election comes.
Newfoundland cannot wait to get after those four who flew in the other day, the four messengers who went down there to try to get the public to accept the budget. They went to the Holiday Inn and spent $4,700. They wasted Liberal Party funds because the 250 people who were there came out shocked and dumbfounded by such a waste of funds by anybody practising restraint. Their glazed salmon and their glazed ministers had to be flown back to Ottawa half-baked, not only glazed, for a vote on Friday afternoon. They were not even there past 1.45 p.m.
I am getting diverted, but my point is that 1 have some sympathy for the amendment which has been suggested by the New Democratic Party. On listening to my own colleagues here, of course, they are a great deal sounder and have a hell of a lot more on the ball than NDP speakers. On listening to the parliamentary assistant, I am prepared to accept the assurance that the ports which are not now supposedly making money will be treated fairly and allowed to operate with a great deal of local independence.
The minister is not all that bad a fellow. He does not listen to most of what I tell him. He ignores my correspondence. It takes him months to get back to me. He does not do what I think he should be doing. But over-all he has a huge department with lots of problems. I ask him to keep an eye on ports like St. John's. They have been discriminated against in the past. I want him to know all the details of my synchrolift. My pet peeve is my synchrolift, which was bludgeoned to death by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) who will be bludgeoned himself in Windsor, I hope, when the next election comes.
Anyway, this being summertime and in the spirit of friendship, I do not want to be partisan today. I just want to make sure that the ports that do not have $100 million of debt-and my hon. friend told me that the Vancouver port had $100 million put aside-will be put on the same basis. Let St. John's owe $100 million and put it aside; put them all on the same basis.

He said: Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief on this one. I started out in committee fighting for four years because the government had included ten years in the bill. Unfortunately we could not get it down to four years, but I believe the government may be inclined to look upon seven years with some favour as a compromise between the ten years and the four years I would have much preferred.
The purpose of my amendment is that nothing concentrates an executive mind more than the thought of his contract running out and perhaps being replaced, if he has not done a job. I found ten years offensive for the simple reason that it is far too long a time. It is almost a sinecure for somebody to sit in a job for ten years. In addition, I have found that the best business brains or the best executives in North America normally suffer from what is known as the five-year syndrome. If they have worked five years in a particular job, they have normally accomplished everything good that they are going to accomplish, and after that period of time they are on the downhill slant.
I think seven years is too long, but I propose my amendment and hope that it will be agreeable, simply again in order that whoever is heading up the ports corporation can at least be gotten rid of in seven years rather than in ten years if they are not effective.
I might also add that there is nothing in the amendment which means a first-rate man could not be reappointed for an additional seven years.

Mr. Speaker, I have just a very brief comment in support of the amendment put forward by the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook). If we read the wording of the bill with respect to the appointment of the chairman of the board of the Canada Ports Corporation, we find that that appointment shall be at the pleasure of the governor in council. Earlier in committee there was some discussion as to what the term "at pleasure" would be interpreted to mean. Our understanding now is that that means a new cabinet could make a change in the person appointed to that position if valid cause were found.
The only problem which was raised in committee was that in most cases a subsidiary contract is entered into between the government or the governor in council and the particular individual selected to manage the corporation, and that that contract could bind the government to keeping that person for the full seven-year term, even if political circumstances, health factors or matters bearing on the competence of that person suggest that he should be removed.
I recommend very strongly to the minister and to the House that the practice of entering into subsidiary contracts makes it possible, albeit undesirable in some cases, for an incompetent administrator to remain in place by pointing to the letter of the law as spelled out in the contract or, conversely, expecting a major severance allowance if the governor in council in its wisdom decides that the person should be removed,
I suggest that the government look carefully at some of the major costs to the taxpayers of Canada which have accrued in the past where it has attempted to remove for one reason or another senior people who have been the beneficiaries of subsidiary contracts. By shortening the term of the appointment to seven years as my hon. colleague is recommending, I think we can help to diminish the adverse aspects of prolonged appointments, but we do not eliminate the problems created by these subsidiary contracts.

Mr. Speaker, I will not speak at any length on this motion. We do not disagree with it. Certainly a seven-year term seems appropriate. I do not entirely disagree with a ten-year term provided that there would be a way for making a reappointment. Certainly the operation of a huge system such as our national ports in Canada requires a good deal of experience.
However, my intention in rising was to point out some of the events which took place in this process. I believe it is rather interesting to note that the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook) was adamant in committee about this bill, and if you read his speech which he gave in the House you will find he said that he thought that this was the worst bill which could possibly have been presented. Suddenly, from behind the scenes, we have the Liberals and the Conservatives getting into these little backroom deals. We see a little compromise, which was drafted up by the government, shown to the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby, who is a dear
Canada Ports Corporation Act
friend of the government, and then presented to the House. I just wanted to point out that all is not as it seems. There are a few bedfellows around here who might be crossing the door.
I must also mention the fact, which is very typical of some hon. members and particularly true of the hon. member who spoke before the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby, that whenever there is a senior position being discussed it is always referred to as "he". The hon. member repeated this throughout our committee experience. Whenever he referred to any of the senior positions in this ports system, it was always "he". Of course, I challenged him several times and said that we needed an affirmative action program in the ports system and a cleansing of the attitude of certain members in the House.
I would also mention that this approach is reinforced in the language of this bill. I know that we cannot deal with that matter today, but we must deal with it at some point because when the language of all these bills is always drafted so that reference is always made to the masculine gender, it reinforces these prejudices and sexist attitudes which assume that a male will always be appointed to these positions. That is all 1 have to say on this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, this is an amusing little debate. I do not think it is earth-shattering but nevertheless it is interesting.
The hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon) mentioned the expenditures which the government must incur when it wants to remove a person, male or female, appointed for a ten-year period. That was the point he was concerned about. This could very well happen. It could happen, indeed, that someone does not perform as he was expected to.
Or she.

He or she was expected to. Thank you.
One could also look at it from the other point of view, with respect to the expenditures a government would have to make in order to appoint a person to a senior office which involved only a short period, such as four or five years in this instance. People who accept those jobs do so at the best time of their lives, generally speaking, and if the job does not give them security for a fairly long period of time the government would have to pay them much more than if it were appointing them for a longer period. This is why a compromise was reached "in the backroom", as the NDP implies, because we thought that a ten-year period might be too long and, hopefully, the opposition realized that four or five years might be too short a time. This is how we arrived at seven years. The reason the government accepted seven years was that, interestingly enough, the most recent trend is toward a seven-year tenure as opposed to a ten-year one. There are two or three recent instances where the government has appointed a chairman and presidents for seven years as opposed to the traditional period.

Mr. Speaker, I still find the Canada ports bill disastrous. It is a terrible bill which gives the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) absolute and total control of the ports. However, through this
amendment, if we can possibly pass it, there will at least be one small shred of local autonomy. I repeat that there will be one minute piece of local autonomy. The key portion, which is in this amendment but which was not in the act, states that a local port corporation will determine its own surplus as a result of this amendment. In the act previous to this amendment everything was determined by either the Canada ports corporation, the senior body or the minister.
It is terribly offensive when there is that kind of absolute power residing in Ottawa and in the hands of the minister. Despite all the government's assurances as to how it will give local autonomy to all the ports, where is it written? It is not written in the act, except in this amendment. At least we cut of the Canada Ports Corporation at the pass. It cannot declare a surplus for a local port corporation by itself. It must have the agreement of the local port corporation for it to be declared a surplus. That is exceedingly important, certainly to the port of Vancouver, and I suspect to many of the other ports. It does give them that little bit more control over their own money which was not in the legislation before this amendment. I wish it could have gone much further.
I still find it offensive that the minister can do any ruddy thing he wants to in terms of a local port corporation or the Canada Ports Corporation. I find it offensive that the minister has the total and absolute authority for all appointments to the boards. It would have been far better had it been set up in such a way that there was local input into these appointments, where the minister had to listen and had to select from people chosen from the local areas. But, no, there is none of that in this bill, either. If one looks at the powers of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) under this Canada ports bill, one will find that he actually has all the local ports corporations and the Canada Ports Corporation under his heel, to do with as he pleases. That is terribly unfortunate for a couple of reasons. One is that if there is a cabinet shuffle this summer, which I would suggest is a possibility, then we will no longer have this Minister of Transport. He will go on to his reward, or to a greater function.
What could that be?

That means that when a new minister of transport decides to do something, we will not be able to question him and say, "But you said-" because all that becomes irrelevant because if he is no longer the minister of transport, the new minister of transport will not have to pay attention to any of his great policies.
To please you, I am willing to stay around.

I might also add that I now find the marine administrator is switching over as soon as he can get rid of this bill. He will leave as well, and will look after airlines and airports rather than being the marine administrator. So, all the
July 26, 1982

promises and statements that he made will no longer be relevant to this legislation.
I am very suspicious as to what is taking place. The men who make the promises, who have done all the lobbying across the country and who have made such grandiose statements about all the local autonomy which is not written in the bill, will no longer be there if the legislation is passed and comes into force. However, if this amendment is accepted, it will mean one small bit of local autonomy for the ports of this nation in terms of a local port corporation determining whether or not it has a surplus. The Canada Ports Corporation will not be able to say it is a surplus, if this amendment passes, and rip it away from the local port corporation. The two corporations will have to agree that there is a surplus. That, mind you, is still only half the war, because the minister will still have the power, as a minister, to declare some of the funds to the local port corporation as surplus and take them. But that would be a much more dangerous political act than it would have been had the Canada Ports Corporation been empowered simply to decide that the money was surplus.
With this amendment, I have at least attempted to gain that small bit of autonomy for the various local ports corporations across the country, and I sincerely hope they appreciate it.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by saying that I do not believe my hon. friend, the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook), meant to be quite as hard on the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) as he perhaps was, because I know how anxious he is to see this particular amendment adopted. We hope that the government, having given full regard to the deliberations in committee, and the strong concerns that several members of the opposition have brought to committee on this particular issue, will have the wisdom to see that this amendment is desirable and positive and should be supported by the government.
There was much emphasis in committee on subclauses 34 and 36 of Clause 13, those subclauses being amendments to the National Harbours Board Act 1936. There were some rather wild statements, notably coming from my colleagues to the left, that all that the Conservative members from Vancouver wanted was to prop up the port of Vancouver and strip away the revenues and profits from all the neighbouring ports which, in fact, was a total mistruth. We are as concerned as anyone about seeing that the ports of Canada are placed on an economically sound basis and that they succeed and prosper individually and collectively, so that in total their surplus revenues can be contributed to a central fund and redisbursed at a fair market rate on the approval of the local port corporation, redisbursed to help with the development of other ports where additional revenues are needed for their capital purposes.
In speaking to the amendment of the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby, which appears as motion No. 5 on the Order Paper, I should just like to point out that there is considerable difference in the wording of this amendment. Even though, perhaps, some might argue that the mechanics are not all that different, the wording is such as to eliminate what I consider to be a red flag waved at people in areas such
Canada Ports Corporation Act
as we come from, where there is far too much of this government holding the line and totally disregarding the views of opposition members, whether they be NDP or Conservative. The people we represent resent this terribly, and if Liberal members opposite really want to understand why it is that western Canadians have virtually totally rejected them in recent years, let me tell them that it is because of this notion that no good ideas could ever come from opposition members, from western Canada, from Atlantic Canada or from north of 60d. In fact, we come to the Parliament and to committee to express legitimate views on behalf of those who sent us here. A legitimate view we have expressed with regard to this particular clause is that, given the present wording, it says that the corporation may, with the approval of the minister, require a local port corporation to make a loan. That wording is essentially a red flag, an aggravation to the persons charged with managing the port of Vancouver and doing business with that port and the general populace who benefits by the very welcome presence of that port, as do their counterpart citizens in other parts of the country.
The hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby suggested that the mandatory nature of Subclause 13(34) be somewhat restrained-in fact, removed-whereby the local port corporation would have the final say as to what should or should not be deemed surplus to its requirements. The amendment provides that the revenues of a local port corporation, after meeting local expenses, interest payments and any other expenses, may be retained by the local port corporation. That is in direct contrast to the wording of subclause 34(1), as written, and I am suggesting that if the government really wants the people of the Vancouver area in British Columbia to feel a little better disposed toward it, this would be the kind of amendment which would certainly go a long way toward helping and resolving some of these deep regional differences. We will be prepared to give the government credit where credit is due, if it is prepared to accept the amendment.
To backtrack slightly, I should say that I, too, am philosophically opposed to the creation of more Crown corporations, particularly a double-layered system where there is a parent corporation and a limitless number of subsidiary Crown corporations, as this bill provides, for a number of reasons which will be brought forward in third reading debate. But, to put it in a nutshell, I think we have Crown corporationitis in this country. We have a number of Crown corporations now growing toward 500. There is a definite lack of accountability in many cases. There are no clear-cut terms of reference as to which ones shall have a public interest mandate and be subsidized and which ones shall be expected to operate on a pay-as-you-go basis. There have been all kinds of scandals involving Crown corporations and refuge to the arm's length provision which allows a minister to deny Parliament the kind of detailed scrutiny that it requires of Crown corporations.
In general 1 find this bill unacceptable, feeling that it can solve all of the problems of the various port authorities by

July 26, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
creating, as it tried to do with the Canada Post Corporation, yet another series or family of Crown corporations to facilitate our national harbours. The ports I know best are Vancouver, Roberts Bank and Prince Rupert. I am told by the local officials that the major objective of bringing forward this legislation at this time is to increase the spending limit to allow officials at the local level to make purchases in response to bids received in the tendering process and to increase the ceiling from $50,000 per item to as much as $10 million. That would go a long way toward facilitating some of the management and long-range planning problems of our local ports.
To be fair, this bill provides for a maximum $10 million spending limit where there are competitive Canadian bids for any single item purchased through the Canada Ports Corporation. That is a step in the right direction. It provides that local ports shall have some proportion of that $10 million spending accorded to them on an individual basis.
We have not had confirmed what the actual ceiling will be. Perhaps in his concluding remarks the minister might indicate what, for example in the case of the ports of Vancouver or St. John's, the actual ceiling spending limit will be at this time according to the guidelines and the criteria which the governor in council is presently preparing.
Second, we were told by officials at the port of Vancouver that they wanted to be able to award leases to tenants on National Harbours Board property. Under the provisions of the present act, they had to have those decisions vetted and finally authorized in Ottawa by the minister, in some cases in consultation with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston). That created a lot of delays. It held up the ports in maintaining the momentum they needed to remain competitive with their United States counterparts on the west coast of North America and, I am sure, equally on the east coast.
I want to say in that regard that those measures alone could have been accommodated by a straightforward amendment to the National Harbours Act 1936. I am sure members of this House would have facilitated the passage of such simple amendments very quickly.
If that were the only objective of this legislation, there would have been no difficulty with members of this party in ensuring that those spending ceilings and the decision-making authority with respect to leases was properly and fully delegated to the local level of port management. In fact, the wording in subclauses 34 and 36 of Clause 13 in the printed version of the bill suggests a consolidation of power and financial control in Ottawa.
The purpose of the amendment put forward by the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby and the separate amendment I put forward as motion No. 6, which would delete entirely subclause 36 is to make it clear that there will in fact be the high degree of local autonomy accorded to the local port corporations, which we heard so much about in committee from the minister and the officials. If it is their intention to
accord this degree of financial sovereignty to the local ports, I urge the government to consider seriously the amendments before them.
At second reading debate, the Minister of Transport confirmed to me, as recorded at page 18825 of Hansard, that the surplus funding which is earned at a particular port, the port of Vancouver in that case, will be available on a first-call basis for the development of the port. That was the wording I used. The minister rose in his place and said it will. I repeated the request for confirmation, and the minister said, "Sure".
We had some fun in committee trying to get the minister's officials to agree that he had in fact committed the government to providing surplus funds to the local ports which earns them a first-call basis, within the framework of the central banking function of the nation, and the notion that in the national interest there may be certain cases where loans should be legitimately extended to other ports through the Canada Ports Corporation.
The amendment put forward by the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby provides the final out to the governor in council that subclause 3, which ensures that if a port is really and truly selfish and decides it is going to prevent the government from drawing that surplus for other purposes, the minister and the governor in council can intervene and ensure that that does not happen. I think the objectives of the government have been accomplished and the concerns we expressed in committee have been satisfied.
Although it is rare to compliment members of the House, it is a fact that the views of the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby are consistent with the requests of many groups in the Vancouver region, in particular the principals of Vancouver Wharves Limited who have written in support of his initiatives to ensure a higher degree of local autonomy and to fight for these amendments to subclauses 34 and 36.
A subsequent telegram was received from the North Vancouver Chamber of Commerce. It states that it is in support of increased autonomy for the port of Vancouver. In the past it had supported Bill C-92, believing it to be a step in the right direction. However, they stated a number of serious reservations and urged the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby to continue to push forcefully for the amendments which culminate in the amendment he has put forward today as motion No. 5.
I know there is a desire to make an announcement momentarily. I would just like to say in conclusion that the most important request of the city of Vancouver has been for an amendment deleting subclause 36, which is provided for in my motion No. 6. That will take away another red flag where the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the governor in council might be able to threaten expropriation of surplus funds. I urge upon the minister and the government that these two amendments put forward as motions Nos. 5 and 6 be adopted.
