Mr. Speaker, perhaps this bill and its amendments will bring to the attention of Canada the total lack of long-term, co-ordinated national planning for a transportation policy. That is the situation in which we find ourselves today. As I said when the bill was debated on second reading, it will depend entirely on the policies and principles of the government that administers it if the ports are to benefit. And as was pointed out by the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook), the present minister will probably administer the bill for some time. I am confident that he will honour his commitment, but I am equally confident that any change in policy reflected by a different minister will negate his present intentions.
We should not lose sight of the fact that this is enabling legislation which leaves control of the ports in the hands of the Department of Transport and the edict of the minister and the policy of the government of the day. That is the basis on which some people in Canada have supported the bill, that is also the weakness which many Canadians fear, and I am amongst that number. We must consider our future potential with regard to our rail system, we are debating how much money should be spent in the long term to transport grain over the Rockies to the markets of the Far East or perhaps even through the Panama canal. In any case it is a long-term and very expensive proposition to put the policy in place.

July 26, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
Should we then relegate some ports, such as Churchill, to a relatively insignificant role under this bill? Unless the government offers some initiatives, the port of Churchill will not play a significant role in the export of grain in the years ahead. The reason for this is that we are at present enchanted with the proposition that ports should make a profit, and if they do not, then as far as this government is concerned, they will be left in the doldrums.
I cite Churchill as an example because as an easterner 1 see it as a kindred spirit of the ports of eastern Canada. I see it as a port which can be useful, but unless government policy supports it, that use will be minimal. It needs the support of rail transportation and improved handling facilities if a great deal of western grain shipments are to be diverted through it.
Some statements have been made in the House to the effect that if a port cannot pay its way it should be closed. We have to look at the cost to Canada of operating ports under the present policy. Perhaps it would be cheaper to spend a little money to increase Churchill's handling capability for grain than to double track or double tunnel the Rocky mountains in order to push more of that grain westward, along with the sulphur, oil and other raw materials which pass over that range. We need a transportation policy to deal with this.
As I have said in the House over the years, we should be looking for multi-purpose cars, and not solely at the idea of unit trains, to move grain westward. We should look at the possibility of unit trains moving grain eastward to the Atlantic ports and examining what a multi-purpose car could do to reduce the necessity for double tracking through the Rockies. It might be cheaper to move 10 million tonnes of grain through the port of Saint John, the port of Halifax or the port of Churchill than to accommodate the double tracking necessary to move additional amounts of raw materials, both grain and natural resources, through the west. This act has totally overlooked the necessity of a national policy and the net cost of transportation to the Canadian people.
Getting down to the individual ports, we have converted from debt to equity a total of approximately $475,342,000. About $231 million of that applies to the port of Montreal, and $99 million to the port of Vancouver. The others have a miscellaneous amount of debt forgiven, such as St. John's at $382,000. That is not very much, and I do not blame the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) for complaining about the treatment of that port. When we pick up the principal, which is still unpaid and which is the responsibility of the ports, we find that the port of Saint John has a balance of $7,281,000 which it will have to pay. The port of Montreal will have to pay $9,470,000. The port of Montreal has a net income of $18,624,000, which will take care of that $9.5 million it owes presently. But the net income of the port of Saint John is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $2 million, with $7 million outstanding. Again, the fairness and equity of the treatment of these two ports is not particularly satisfactory. The port of
Vancouver has a net operating income of $17,687,000, with other income of $7,959,000. With that income, the port of Vancouver is in pretty good shape under most circumstances. Then there is the port of Montreal with an operating income of $10,685,000 and other income of $7,939,000, for a net income of $18,624,000. Those ports are very well looked after.
Let us then, Mr. Speaker, take a look at the indebtedness of the port of Halifax and the port of Saint John and compare them with their means. We find that in both ports the balance is not there. I am sorry the minister has left the House, and I appreciate he cannot be here all the time, but the port of Saint John has an operating income of $1,522,000 and other income of $637,000, for a total of $2,159,000 as its operating revenue. That means that the port of Montreal has more cash flow than all the other ports in Eastern Canada and less debt to pay back than the port of Saint John.
Therefore, I am going to repeat my request to the House and the minister to reconsider the position they have taken. The port of Saint John happens to be the only one with debt other than what it owes to the National Harbours Board and the Government of Canada.
I want to read a wire forwarded by the mayor of Saint John to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) at 3.55 p.m., July 8, 1982. It reads as follows:
Strongly suggest that remaining $22 million loan by Province of New Brunswick to construct Rodney Terminal in Saint John be forgiven and thus allow Port of Saint John to operate the same as other ports under National Harbours Board jurisdiction, prior to new ports policy becoming law.
When I raised this in committee I was told by the minister, that, well, we might have a trade-off. New Brunswick owes us, we owe New Brunswick, let us cancel our debts. Mr. Speaker,
I do not accept that and I never proposed that as a way in which $22 million could be paid on behalf of the port of Saint John. That is because when I pick up the report of the National Harbours Board as it relates to the St. Lawrence area I find that they spent, in a single year in the port of Montreal, $16 million on one structure, $19.7 million on another, $3 million on another-
That is money provided by the port of Montreal itself.
Well now, this seems to be under the auspices of the National Harbours Board.
That is it.
The money which comes from the NHB, until the passage of this act, has been money which belonged to the people of Canada, and they had to vote to spend that money.
But of course the money comes from the port of Montreal, that is a fact.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think that is really a fair interjection by the minister, and he has been abundantly fair over the years. That remark ignores the fact that the Port of Montreal has received two or three parcels of land as a gift
July 26, 1982

or for the nominal sum of $1, and that land is generating revenue approaching $8 million a year which goes into the cash flow of the port of Montreal. When you compare that with the cash flow of other ports in Eastern Canada, those ports are in a position of disadvantage. When you compare the fact that we are talking about user pay and we have the St. Lawrence Seaway which does not pay its way, and a St. Lawrence River which cannot function without icebreakers, and that is not charged to the port of Montreal or other ports on the St. Lawrence River, and then you add to that the additional pilotage charges which take place over a much more extended area in the St. Lawrence than in any other area in Canada, I submit to you that the port of Montreal and those other ports in the St. Lawrence Valley are getting advantages that no other ports anywhere in Canada get.
Hear, hear!

All I ask for, Mr. Speaker, is fair play. And as the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. Leblanc) sits in his seat and smiles at me, I submit that he and the other members from Atlantic Canada should take up the cudgel because there should be no indebtedness on the part of any port anywhere in Canada to any government in Canada.
Hear, hear!
I did not smile at you, don't kid yourself. I was smiling at the hon. minister.

You would smile at him because he has really not dealt fairly with the ports of Atlantic Canada. You are a minister and you are a party to it. Along with the other six Liberal members from New Brunswick you have forgotten about New Brunswick, whether it be over Via Rail or the ports of Canada; whether it be the fishing ports or the NHB ports. That member, Mr. Speaker, was associated with the Liberal Party when the port of Saint John had to go begging to the province to get its piers. If it had not got the money from the province, there would be no container terminal and no forest terminal because this government was not prepared to vote the money to put them there.
Don't rewrite history.

I am not jealous of the port of Montreal; I am just concerned about the inequity. The government forgives $211 million of debt for Montreal and only peanuts, relatively speaking, to the rest of the ports in Canada. You talk about user pay and how the ports must operate on their own cash flow. The port of Montreal has nearly $19 million in cash flow and the port of Saint John has so much less that it is not even funny. In addition, it has a provincial debt which it has to liquidate over a period of time at a rate to be negotiated.
That is not the way it ought to be. The Government of Canada has to take a look at the assorted needs of Canada. It should take a look at the requirements of Newfoundland, of
Canada Ports Corporation Act
Prince Edward Island, of New Brunswick and at its commitment to the tuna plant in Saint John, New Brunswick. The government's commitment was to extend the harbour if the plant were expanded. We now find that the expansion of the harbour at the Champlain industrial park is under consultation and all the ports of eastern Canada are to be studied by some unknown consultant. The decision as to whether or not the government will keep its word to the tuna plant in St. Andrews depends upon a report of a consultant.
The tuna plant acted in good faith and undertook its expansion which required additional port facilities. I raised this matter in the proceedings of the committee, but I got no answer. I had to find out from external sources, from occasional appointments of mine, who said "1 am working on a consulting plan to determine whether money will be spent on the ports" I asked whether the one in the Champlain industrial park was included, and the answer given to me was yes. I mentioned that a commitment had been made by the Government of Canada that if the tuna plant expanded, the harbour facility would be expanded. The answer I received was, "It is under my jurisdiction in a study".
Why the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans supports this bill and this government is beyond my comprehension. I say this as a New Brunswicker. 1 challenge the minister to be one. I submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that if he is a good, solid and loyal New Brunswicker the Government of Canada will send a cheque to the port of Saint John to send to the province of New Brunswick so as to put that port at least on a comparable basis of indebtedness. There will not be a search for a change of liabilities. There will be a cheque to relieve that indebtedness which is unique in the ports of Canada. I plead with you as a New Brunswicker, Mr. Minister, to get a cheque for the port of Saint John to pay the province of New Brunswick. You have bullwhipped the province into making the money because you would not spend it in the first place. You have now left the port in a position of indebtedness that is comparable to no other port anywhere in Canada. Let us get equality for New Brunswick and the port of Saint John.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) entertain a question?
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

I must say that both in committee and in the House my colleagues and I have been very impressed with the statements made by the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte. We are most impressed with his sincerity and concern about ports in New Brunswick and in the Maritimes provinces. But when he spoke earlier about the port of Churchill, I wondered, being quite sympathetic to its financial needs, does he agree with the statement made by the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook) earlier today when he said, "if Churchill cannot be financially self-sufficient, it should be shut down"?

Mr. Speaker, having entertained the question I must have permission to answer it. I have to say that if the

July 26, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
hon. member would interpret the remark in the spirit in which it was given in relation to the idea that the ports of Canada have to be self-sustaining, he was challenging the government to close it. He was not saying close the port of Churchill. He wast just challenging the government to close if if it did not pay its way. God knows, we need the port of Churchill as well as the Atlantic ports.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make some comments with respect to the amendment before us. This is an amendment that we can support very strongly. It is one that both opposition parties were repeatedly advocating in committee. It is of particular concern as outlined in a number of documents from the port of Vancouver, but I am sure the matter is of concern to other ports as well, namely that local port corporations to be really autonomous must have control over their own funds to the greatest degree possible.
It is interesting that this motion actually presented by the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook) replaces six of his previous amendments presented in committee, many of which we would have supported here, and all of which concern local port autonomy. We do feel that the amendment before us fulfils the concerns we had expressed in committee that local port corporations should control their revenues to the greatest degree possible for operating costs, for the cost of borrowing if that should be needed, and for capital projects. I think when we talk about capital projects we have to talk about the short term, the five and six-year plans which have to be budgeted very specifically. We also have to talk about the long-range plans. The port of Vancouver's master plan is one example. We agree that surplus funds which are generated by the port over and above operating costs should be retained by that port for any capital costs. We agree also with the central banking concept. In fact, we had an amendment in committee which spelled this out. Instead of the parent corporation, the Canada Ports Corporation would be able to cream off the excess funds, which it perhaps thought were surplus, for use in the general port system. This should be done only in consulation and with complex approval of the local port corporation.
We would like to see the central banking concept spelled out a little more. We certainly need to see more of the bylaws as well for capital funds that we were told in committee would be available over and above the surplus funds generated by any one port.
Although we support this motion, we do not have complete confidence that we have full information. We will look with great interest at the bylaws when they are ready.
I would like to spend a minute on the first section as it applies to the port of Vancouver. The port of Vancouver has specifically requested a change in the procedure for control of local funds. On June 30, 1982, the mayor of Vancouver forwarded to the committee a statement as follows:
*-Any funds transferred from a local port corporation to the parent Corporation would be treated as if they were deposited in a bank, to earn interest and to be subject to withdrawal by the local port depositor when they are required.
This requirement was achieved. We are very pleased also with the concern that was expressed in a telex just a few days ago. That concern surrounded subclause 36 which reads:
The Minister and the Minister of Finance may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, require the corporation to pay to the Receiver General as revenues of Canada so much of the money administered by it as the Minister and the Minister of Finance consider to be in excess of the amount required for the purposes of the corporation.
This is of particular concern because surplus funds are needed not only for a five-year plan but also for a 30-year major master plan which is being developed in co-operation with all municipalities and community groups concerned with this port. We feel those two concerns have been dealt with in this amendment. We also agree with subclause 2 that the corporation may borrow excess funds from the local port corporation, excess in this case being defined more specifically as excess funds being determined by mutual agreement between the local port and the Canada Ports Corporation. In previous statements it was really left to the parent corporation to decide this.
I might also say that the Vancouver city council requested an appeal procedure in this bill which has not been included. Perhaps it is not needed now that the local port corporation has been given more say. As I said before, we are not completely convinced. All of this may not be in writing but certainly in principle it appears to be there, along with the central banking concept, with which we agree, provided the moneys are lent and are still designated as being available to the local port corporation.
We were concerned in committee, and are still as concerned as the Official Opposition, about what rate of interest funds would gather when they are borrowed from the local ports corporation for revenues for the total port system of Canada. We advocate the market interest rate as being fair.
Under the second subpoint of this amendment, we believe it is only fair that when ports have income in excess of their immediate needs, these funds should be available to the port system as a whole. This makes sense, just as when a local port needs additional funding from the parent corporation, they should also be able to get this kind of help.
Fairness means that a national ports policy requires sharing and that the funds should be available in a sensible way for reasonable modernization of ports, which is certainly needed in most instances where there is income over and above operating costs.
In short, we would agree with this amendment, but in closing I would mention just for reference purposes some of the things that are being proposed. Again I will use my own riding port, the port of Vancouver, as an example. From the point of view of the short-term port plan, a $51 million program was just approved by the minister for the port of Vancouver. This includes something over $35 million for dredging contracts for expansion of the Roberts Bank coal port. A total of over $ 11
July 26, 1982

million will be spent at Vanterm over three years to improve its container crane capacity. At the Lynnterm facility another $3.3 million will be spent to expand and modernize that development. Also it includes a new Burrard Street viaduct to which the federal government contributed over $1 million. Of course we can see that modern and large international ports have many expenditures which have to be covered with funds in excess of those they can generate from their own income.
As to the long-term development of the port, the master plan of Vancouver already highlights the following findings. I will just skim over them to put on the record the very broad kinds of development which will have to be funded over the next 30 years for major development of a very important international port. Air transportation will need to be expanded by the provision of an additional helicopter landing and take-off area. There will have to be an expansion of coal handling facilities within the port area by the provision of additional terminal capability. In the area of coastal shipping, current traffic volumes are expected to level off. This is of increasing significance to all the problems of British Columbia. Continued growth is predicted in commercial fishing for various firms in the port of Vancouver. There will be significant growth in the demand for container handling within the port area. I am sure that this is the case in other major ports of Canada. New cruise ship facilities will replace the temporary facilities, and federal government funds are needed for this development. I think members from my area will admit that additional federal grants are needed for this.
Also it will cost money to provide environmental statutes applicable to the port area. Physical improvements are needed in the areas of excursion boating, forest products handling, general cargo handling and grain products handling. Physical improvements are also needed to expand greatly the grain terminal facilities and railroad capabilities. In the area of hydrocarbons handling, current terminal facilities have significant potential for increased volumes. Substantial growth is predicted in terms of potash handling.
In the area of public recreation, we need major changes in land use around the port. Some community groups are very concerned about this. There must be more access to the port for communities, and there must be a change in some of the present lease arrangements over the next period of long-term planning. There must be upgrading and expansion of the rail system. There are considerable hasards in the port which I have personally witnessed driving around it. Additional marinas are proposed for recreational boating facilities. In terms of road access it is important to have municipal and regional input into planning for the port.
Also I wish to mention sulphur handling and support activities such as those to which my colleague referred when he spoke about the entire marine industrial strategy or plan for marine industrial development, whichever term one chooses to use.
All these things are extremely important in the development of our ports. In the case of the port of Vancouver, they will not only take considerable planning, but will certainly need long-
Canada Ports Corporation Act
term allocation of funds from those funds generated by the port as well as perhaps from additional loans through the parent corporation. We support this amendment, as I say, and we support it particularly because of the needs of the port of Vancouver.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to address myself to the subject of the management of some of our ports in Canada because that, of course, is the topic of the motion now before the House. In particular I refer to the situation at the port of Happy Valley in Goose Bay, Labrador, in my own province. This situation cries out for correction and improvement. I am referring to a port which is administered directly by the Department of Transport. In that port the Government of Canada and its agency, CN Marine, have allowed a situation to arise that cries for correction, a situation which permits a monopoly on all freight going into Goose Bay and on all freight or cargo moving out of Goose Bay by a person who is a well-connected friend of the government.
Let me explain some of the background of this situation. The person 1 am talking about is Mr. Melvin Woodward who was a Liberal member of the House of Assembly of Newfoundland for the Goose Bay-Happy Valley area for a number of years. He was defeated in 1975. He ran again as the Liberal candidate in the June 1979 election and again in the April 1982 election, and was defeated both times. He is a close political associate of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey). He has been made director of the Bank of Canada appointed by the government opposite. He has been made chairman of the Enterprise Development Board for Newfoundland and Labrador by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray). That is just his background.
Until 1980 this same gentleman was the wharfinger at Goose Bay appointed by the Government of Canada. While he was a wharfinger there, he was also in business for himself. One of his businesses was the operation of an oil tanker which delivered oil along the Labrador coast. Since 1973 he has controlled all the stevedoring facilities and services in the Goose Bay-Happy Valley area of Labrador. He was given by the Department of Transport all the sheds and wharfs owned by that department in Goose Bay under a management agreement of 1973. No tenders were called, no lease proposals were called. This particular individual was simply given by the Department of Transport all available sheds and wharfs in the Goose Bay area to use for his own business. In other words, publicly-owned facilities were given to him. For example, Department of Transport shed No. 4 went to Woodward's Limited and sheds Nos. 1, 2 and 5 went to Coastal Shipping Limited. Both companies were owned by the same Melvin Woodward without any tenders being called. In addition, from the year 1969 onward, without any tenders ever being called, this same Melvin Woodward was given the job to do all of the stevedoring for CN Marine in Goose Bay-Happy Valley. The main shipping service to Goose Bay-Happy Valley-not the only service but the main essential one-is CN Marine. This

July 26, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
government agency, also without calling tenders, also without calling proposals, has had Mr. Woodward act as its stevedore in the Goose Bay-Happy Valley area and as its agent in that area since 1969.
In addition to this, he controls all of the facilities, he controls the wharves, he controls the sheds. No one has put in a proposal as stevedore because they cannot get the sheds and the use of the wharves which are controlled by Woodward. When you make a complaint that this is the situation, CN Marine will say that it has to deal with Woodward. Nobody else can have access to the wharves or the sheds. When you complain to the Department of Transport it says that it has to deal with Woodward. He is the stevedore for CN Marine. The man is safely covered on all sides.
What is the point I am coming to in connection with all of these arrangements made with this Liberal agent, Mr. Woodward? I wrote to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) about this situation on November 26, 1981, bringing all of this to his attention. The reason I brought this to his attention was that it had been brought to my attention that Mr. Woodward, in addition to being paid by CN Marine for all of these stevedoring services in the Goose Bay-Happy Valley area, was also charging a terminal fee, as he called it, to everyone who receives cargo in the Goose Bay-Happy Valley area. All inbound cargo was subject to this terminal fee for a terminal that is owned by the public, paid for by the public money. This private individual was charging a terminal fee last year of S5.20 for every tonne of cargo that he unloaded as CN Marine's stevedore at Goose Bay. He then charged everyone in the Goose Bay area who shipped cargo out of the area a terminal charge of $5.20 a tonne to put it on board the CN ships he stevedored for, or any other ships.
He does this without any right whatsoever. He does not own the wharves and he does not own the sheds. He has been given them by the government without any tenders ever being called. This Mr. Woodward and his companies are charging this terminal fee of $5.20 a tonne.
Last year, approximately 40,000 tonnes of cargo went into Goose Bay and out during the shipping season, which lasts only some six months because of the ice problems during the period from November until late May each year. In other words, the consumers of the Goose Bay-Happy Valley area were forced to pay over $200,000 unnecessarily in terminal charges to this Liberal agent. The government has put him in a position, with the help of CN Marine, to have a monopoly. He has improperly charged over $200,000 last year in terminal charges made possible by his cozy arrangements with the Liberal Party represented in the Government of Canada and under the instructions-with his background with CN Marine-of the government agency.
Last year, the terminal charge was $5.20 a tonne. This year, the man has the audacity to charge $5.85 a tonne for a terminal fee because of present inflation. In other words, the unjustified fee is up to $5.85 a tonne for every tonne of cargo moved by this gentleman. This year he will charge the consumers of that area in excess of $240,000, to which he is not entitled.
Dealing with the administration of ports, as long as this kind of blatant political partisanship, patronage and corruption is to rule in our courts, we can pass whatever kind of legislation we want because the situation will never be improved. I wrote to the minister on November 26, 1981, and brought this to his attention. I wrote to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) and brought this monopoly situation to his attention. I also wrote to the president of CN and the president of CN Marine to bring it to their attention. After a period of several months I had a reply from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Of course, his reply would only make one laugh if it did not make one cry. He had to concede that there was a monopoly but could not concede that the monopoly is damaging the public for very specious reasons which I do not have time to go into in detail. I would refer to his letter of February 1, 1982, where he said that one of the reasons that the sheds did not go to public tender was that Woodward had the stevedoring contract in Goose Bay and they were consequently leased to Woodward because he was the most likely one to use the sheds for freight distribution. That was the reason the minister gave for giving Mr. Woodward all of those sheds. He should have the sheds because he is going to be doing the stevedoring.
When I went after CN Marine, I had a meeting with Mr. Tingley on May 5, 1981, about this situation. He gave me a different version. He said that CN Marine had to give Woodward the stevedoring contract because he controlled the sheds. Here we have the Government of Canada, through the minister's colleague, saying that it has to give Woodward the sheds and it is not a monopoly because he has the stevedoring contract. Then we have CN Marine saying that it has to give this man stevedoring because he has the sheds. Why can the Department of Transport and CN Marine not get together and call tenders on both of these contracts so that Mr. Woodward is not in a position to be a monopolist and charge what he likes to the consumers of the Happy Valley-Goose Bay area?
Of course, I also got a reply from the minister himself. I believe the reply was dated March 15 and in it he gave all kinds of reasons why this was quite proper and nothing could be done about it. Everything was above board, and of course he did not answer any of the points I made in my letter to him.
Incidentally, I also had a response from CN Marine on January 29, 1982, telling me that CN Marine's responsibility ends when the load is placed on the wharf. CN Marine said, "We are not involved in the setting or collection of terminal and/or delivery charges." In other words, CN Marine does not care how much this man bilks the consumers of the Happy Valley-Goose Bay area. Their responsibility ends when he, their stevedore, takes the cargo from their vessel and puts it on the wharf. Do you know something else? It is not their vessel. It is a vessel supplied by the very same Mr. Woodward. The vessel is called the MV Astron. CN Marine allegedly called for tenders in January of 1981-very short notice to everyone but Mr. Woodward-and manoeuvred the situation so that Mr. July 26, 1982

Woodward won the tender to supply the roll-on roll-off vessel that now carries cargo and freight from St. John's to Louis-porte to Happy Valley-Goose Bay. Therefore, Mr. Woodward, goes to his own vessel, takes the cargo off his own vessel provided to him through CN Marine, lands it through his own stevedoring services on public wharves which he controls, puts them in public sheds which he has been given control of by the Liberal Party of Canada and then charges a terminal charge of $5.85 a tonne when he delivers it to a consumer or when the consumer comes to get this cargo.
This is a situation that cries for correction. A 20-tonne container landed in St. John's, Newfoundland, will be delivered in any area within a 25 mile radius of the port for $75. That fee covers delivery, picking up the container and returning it to the wharf. But at Goose Bay where Mr. Woodward does all of his work and where no one else can do it since he has the monopoly, if you have your container moved several miles you have to pay $200 plus the terminal charge of $5.85 per tonne to have that container moved. That is three times the fee charged in St. John's and you must pay a terminal charge on top of that. I have been corresponding with the Minister of Transport and other ministers for over a year now but they do nothing about this situation. It is a situation that stinks and cries for correction.
Finally, the people of the Goose Bay-Happy Valley area have caught on. On December 1, 1981, a Goose Bay sales company wrote to Mr. Woodward refusing to pay the terminal fee and asked him how he could justify the charge. They have never heard back from him. On May 12, 1982, 20 business firms in the Goose Bay area wired the Minister of Transport about this situation. They have not heard back from him, as far as I know. At the same time, the minister of northern affairs in the Government of Newfoundland, who is the member for that district, wrote to the minister on May 25, and on January 3, 1982, this year, I wrote to the minister again bringing this whole matter to his attention.
We can pass all the legislation we like in the House, but if this kind of conniving, corruption, patronage and trickery is to go ahead, and if no one will do anything about it, then all the legislation we pass in the House does not matter a tinker's damn. The people of the Goose Bay-Happy Valley area are being skinned alive. They already have a very high cost of living. They are living in the north and in a situation where, for six months a year, they get nothing brought in except by air, and then, when the ice goes and the port opens up, we find this Liberal manufactured monopolist putting the boots to them, charging everything under the sun, using his own vessel, chartered by CN Marine, providing the stevedoring services, using a public service, for which he pays little or no rent, and then charging, on top of everything else, a terminal fee of $5.85 a tonne.
I am putting this on public record and asking for a commission of investigation, an inquiry into this corrupt situation in Goose Bay-Happy Valley. I am asking for that inquiry to go on and to inquire into the whole situation with respect to CN Marine, which is out of the control of this government or of
Canada Ports Corporation Act
any government. It had never had a public audit until 1979, all its deficits until then being met by the Government of Canada, and the matter now cries out for public investigation. I understand that the Auditor General is taking special pains this year to attempt to find out what is going on with CN Marine and the cozy arrangements into which CN Marine is entering.
What is some other evidence of favouritism for this Mr. Woodward, this director of the Bank of Canada, this chairman of the Enterprise Development Board, this ex-Liberal candidate, this ex-Liberal member of the House of Assembly in Newfoundland, this buddy, this friend, this campaign manager of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey)? They are heart to heart, soul to soul.
What else is going on with Mr. Woodward? He has had the stevedore contracts from 1968, not just from 1969. There was a building, No. S-1291, which was supposed to be removed from the site and the site restored in 1969. Mr. Woodward was given the building and given permission to leave the building on site when another well-known Newfoundlander was minister of transport, so that building is still there on the site. He is supposed to be paying rental of $177.60 a year for land 40 feet by 148 feet from June 1, 1971. He is actually using land measuring 270 feet by 280 feet and should be paying at least $2,268 per annum, which is another act of favouritism shown to this gentleman.
In September, 1974, a 12,000-barrel fuel tank was placed below high water mark adjacent to the main dock. It was supposed to be cut up and removed by the same Mr. Woodward. It is still there. It has not been cut up and it has not been removed. The storage area to the rear of all those sheds are on a Woodward scrapyard. He pays nothing to the government for that privilege. He has stored it, free, on federal property, since August 7, 1980, whenever he wished, despite the fact that in a memo dated November 10, 1978, it is forbidden for scrap to be stored on federal wharves or approaches. The ordinary federal rules of the Department of Transport do not apply to this self-same Mr. Woodward. Why? Because he is a Liberal. Why? Because he is friend, companion and campaign manager for the Minister of National Revenue. So if he piles the scrap on federally-owned land, on approaches to the wharves and behind the sheds, it does not matter.
There is another major aspect, the Astron. I would need much more time to go into the details of this vessel, the Astron, and how Mr. Woodward got the Astron chartered by CN Marine. That vessel is getting the highest charter hire of any vessel of CN at sea, $4,868 a day on a five-year charter, the most generous charter that CN Marine ever gave, supposedly the result of a tender call, but the tender call laid down certain conditions that all others thought applied, or that Woodward knew did not apply. Therefore, he was the only one to tender the kind of vessel which they afterwards said they wanted. Not only is he getting $4,868 a day for charter hire but he is also getting escalation. Last year he received $4,800 a day. This year he receives a daily charter hire of $4,800 a day

July 26, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
plus 60.1 per cent of the 1982 cost of living index increase. In other words, the cost of living rose 12 per cent, so he will now receive 60.1 per cent of 12 per cent added on to the $4,800 a day. CN guarantees to use his vessel at least 183 days a year. If it cancels the charter during this five-year period, it must purchase the vessel. Therefore, the vessel in the tender call has said, "Canadian-owned and registered vessel preferred". The vessel is bid and registered in Bermuda. It is foreign-owned. It is not a Canadian vessel. But it does not have to pay pilotage fees. It is given a special arrangement with respect to pilotage fees. Mr. Woodward does not hire CBRT or union crews on this vessel. No, he has his own crews on his vessel, permitted by CN Marine, and he paid his seamen $4.10 an hour last year. That is what the Woodward seamen on this vessel received.
I wrote the minister about all this. I know that my time is up, Mr. Speaker, so I will conclude now. I will never conclude with this issue, though, until it is resolved and investigated and a proper report is made.
Hear, hear!

1 wrote the minister about all this, and he sloughed me off. He apparently believed the people whom he sent out to look into this. He told me there was insufficient evidence of improper practices to warrant instructing CN Marine not to go forward with the charter of the vessel, the Astron. The minister took no action to stop that deal going forward. Mr. Minister, this situation cries out for rectification. I do not care if it concerns a Liberal, a Conservative or whoever it is. No person in Canada should be put in this position, to monopolize everything, and then to give the consumers and the ordinary people of Labrador a drubbing and a screwing as this man has been giving them for a number of years, imposing charges that are unwarranted and which have been made possible by the inactivity, if not the active misfeasance, of the government which sits opposite.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I will be brief because most of the remarks I wanted to make have already been made by others. I wanted to note that one of the eminent predecessors of the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin), the late C. D. Howe, was responsible in 1936 for the National Harbours Act that we have today. At that time, the argument in favour of centralization was that the autonomous harbours were riddled with political patronage. I see now that the idea is to go back or revert to the pre-1936 arrangements. We have just seen an illustration of some of the patronage that still exists within the operation of Canadian harbours.
I wanted to endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) with respect to the port of Churchill. It seems ludicrous to me that we do not develop that port, instead of allowing the harbour to silt up, and that we do not adequately maintain the railway track. It is a thousand miles shorter, from the Canadian prairies to Europe through the port of Churchill, than it is through the Lakehead and the
St. Lawrence. That port should be used to a much greater extent than it is at present.
But the point I really wanted the Minister of Transport to hear was with respect to the possible development of a national harbour. Somewhere along the Arctic coast, facing the Beaufort Sea we should develop a national harbour since a number of vessels are operating in that area and the development is dislocated. One company will go in there and do a little bit of dredging and make temporary harbour facilities in one location. A couple of years later they will move over to another place. Do we not have one central location in that area where we might make a national harbour at some time in the future?
What I am suggesting to the minister is that he request his officials to examine that area, 500 or 600 miles of coast from the Alaskan boundary over to the Paulatuk area and locate potential sites for national harbours in that region. They are very limited. Most of the shore of the Beaufort Sea is very shallow way out into the water. There are only one or two limited sites which would make a good national harbour. I suggest we examine those potential sites and have the lands set aside at this time for the development of a national harbour. I hope that can be done. Those are the few comments I want to make. I will not delay the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) any longer.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to make a few comments on motions Nos. 5 and 6. Before I comment on motion No. 5, let me say that before the dinner hour the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook) referred to the role that Gordon Sinclair, the marine administrator, had played with regard to this bill. 1 agree with my hon. friend and I emphasize that the role played by Mr. Sinclair was considerable, if not enormous, in the preparation of this bill.
I also want to praise the four musketeers-as usual, there were five-Messrs. McPherson, Boyer, Innes, Simmons and Biron, chairmen respecting the port authorities at Vancouver, Montreal, St. John's, Halifax and Quebec, who served as advisers in the preparation of this bill.
Back to work, the government is willing to accept motion No. 5. There is nothing here that is very different from what was intended. I agree that the final text, which had many authors, is more clear than the one we started with. Subclause 34 of Clause 13 deals with the so-called banker concept. That is the capacity of the Canada Ports Corporation, the maxi corporation, to act as banker for the local port corporation with respect to their excess or surplus funds. This received considerable interest in the committee, I would say excessive. I doubt whether it will be one of the main sources of financing for ports in the future simply because the concept of surplus or excess funds comes in only after the port corporation has foreseen expenditure for the six-year capital budget.
That is a long time. They will need a lot of money to do that. I would think that a port which finds itself in this position
July 26, 1982

might think of reducing its rates or tariffs in order to attract more customers. Therefore, I do not see it as a major feature of this bill. Be that as it may, it has been substantially improved.
I repeat, Motion No. 5 makes it clearer. The first subclause states the principle very well after providing for five items that the local port corporation has to provide for. The key words are, "Be retained by the local port corporation". That is, the funds will be retained by the local port corporation which, as the hon. member said, is the principle. The first call is for the local port corporation. The words that apply in this amendment are taken from Bill C-50 of 1979.
Subclause 2 makes it clear that the loan from the local port corporation to the Canada Ports Corporation is by agreement between the two entities, the national and the local. I grant to my hon. friend that that is an improvement. It is much friendlier in that fashion than in the previous version. In this instance the minister is left out. The minister comes back in in subclause (3). He can require a local port corporation to loan to the Canada Ports Corporation as usual, taking into account the demands of a six-year budget and after consultation with the local port corporation. That is a better draft. Therefore, we will pass it as an interesting improvement of the bill.
It is a similar situation with Motion No. 6, which deals with subclause (36) of Clause 13. Here the right of the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Finance is affirmed to require the corporation to make a contribution to the Receiver General. Members on the other side did not like that. Because it is not essential to this bill, for the simple reason that that clause is found in the Financial Administration Act, I am not unwilling to depart from it, if such is the wish of the House. However, I want to be very emphatic. There is no change to the reality of it. It is a matter of perception. It is one of the residual powers of the Crown that it can grab money wherever it can grab it. That is expressed in the Financial Administration Act.
The same clause plus is also found in the Harbour Commissions Act. It has never been used. Therefore, this is no great change, and I would not like to present it as such.
As I said in committee, that clause was in the bill because we wanted to accommodate the possibility that the Canada Ports Corporation and local port corporation might move from Schedule C under the Financial Administration Act to Schedule D and then, like CN and Air Canada, they would have to make a contribution to the government by way of dividends. This is the clause in the Financial Administration Act that permits the minister and the government to extract dividends from Schedule D Crown corporations. That was one of the reasons it was there.
I repeat, this is not being taken out. It is found in Section 71(4) of the Financial Administration Act. If I had time I would read it. This is no great change. It is a perception only, as some of my friends opposite have said.
I would like to spend a lot of time on this but I will not do that. I am not entitled to speak for a long time, as is the hon.
Canada Ports Corporation Act
member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). If I did that, I would be considered uncouth, uncivilized and unfriendly. Therefore, I will not. I want to give everyone a chance to speak, including the chairman of the Transport Committee of this House who did such a good job on this bill. I want everyone to have a chance to speak.
I want to say a few words only in reply to the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain). He talked about the need for money in Saint John, New Brunswick. It was interesting to observe that members did not resist the temptation to go regional, an unfortunate characteristic in this country. That does not apply to the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) who is an exception in everything he does.
One of the members from Vancouver talked about the large expenditures in the port of Vancouver. That is all from savings from funds originating in the port of Vancouver. Similarly, expenditures in the port of Montreal are all from savings made in that port. In Halifax, for example, the federal government recently invested $20-some million dollars in Fairview Cove. Similarly, in Saint John it was $29 million. There is a distinction to be drawn between funds originating from the revenues of the local ports and funds originating from federal contributions. Be that as it may, with respect to Saint John I said in the committee that it is not easy for me to forgive that particular debt. First of all, this is not a money bill, and I could not do it in this bill. Second, that debt is the result of a loan by the Government of New Brunswick to the port. In other instances the contributions of the provinces have come to ports by way of grants, so that if we were going to compensate the province of New Brunswick for a loan contribution to the port of Saint John, all the other provinces-and there are many which have made grant contributions to their ports-would come and say, "What the heck; are we going to be penalized because we were more generous, possibly, than the Government of New Brunswick?" My hon. friend should realize that there is a problem here. In the committee I extended myself fully in relation to the concept about which he smiles now, which is an arrangement by which Peter might pay Paul. We are still working at that, even if we do not have the gratitude of the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte.
With respect to the contribution of the hon. member for St. John's West about the Goose Bay terminal, I could go on almost as long as he did.
I was getting started.

I hesitate to do that, for very good reasons. This is really the equivalent of a vendetta between the Montagues and the Capulets, and I hesitate to put my finger between the tree and the bark. It seems that one of the mistakes Mr. Woodward has made has been to challenge the strength and power of the Crosbies in that particular area, and presumably that is his punishment.

July 26, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
That is complete junk. It is the public being screwed up there; it has nothing to do with the Crosbies. You are going to regret that.

The information I have is that Coastal Shipping has a bona fide contract with CN Marine, and with respect to the Department of Transport, since 1980-I do not know about the time before that; my hon. friend is possibly right about that-Transport Canada has applied the principle of tendering in renting property. The famous shed 1, shed 2, shed 3 and shed 5-
They haven't called tenders.
Yes, Coastal has a three-year lease now.
But they have never called tenders for it. They were given it.
The information I have is that this was done on a tendering basis.
Ten years before that what happened?
1 am not talking about ten years before. I am just saying that, contrary-
No tenders have ever been called.

-to what my hon. friend says, since 1980 the lease has been on a tender basis with Coastal Shipping. In any event, it is slightly different from what the hon. member said on this particular matter. The rental was based on market value as determined by the Department of Public Works.
Market value? Junk. Tell us what the rent is.
That is one opinion. I do not have the detail of what the rent is.
Of course you don't.

I have written to the hon. member before. My hon. friend referred to that. I will be writing him again after another inquiry, which has been conducted, is completed. 1 understand that the president of CN Marine, Mr. Armstrong, has already written to the hon. member on this subject. This is what I know on this matter. I am very concerned that justice should be done and justice should be seen to be done, and I will continue my research so that my hon. friend will not have reasons for grievance the way he had tonight.
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the minister would entertain a question.
Yes.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the minister why, in the absence of intelligent ports policy historically, he should now use the Old Testament biblical policy that the sins of the fathers should be visited upon the sons and that the debt should remain the debt of the port of Saint John. If the
minister feels that conscience dictates that other provinces should be reimbursed, why not reimburse them all? That is my question.
Mr. Speaker, I have already explained well why it is difficult to forgive the loan made to the port. I explained that well, I thought.
Why ask the sons to bear the sins of the fathers in the old biblical sense?

Again, I will repeat that one of the main reasons is that in this particular instance the province of New Brunswick made a loan to the port. In other instances-for example, in Nova Scotia with respect to Fairview Cove-it was a grant or gift. In British Columbia, at Prince Rupert, similarly, it was a gift. We cannot easily pay back New Brunswick for a loan because those provinces which made grants-gifts-would come back and say they deserve the same repayment. I think this is not illogical.
You did not answer the question. That's all.
I thought I had, but I will try again next time.
Why should the sins of the fathers be visited on the sons on the Old Testament biblical "eye for an eye" basis?

That is not really the intent. In addition to that, the port of Saint John has done rather well. The potash development which has taken place is sponsored by the federal government at the level of $29 million, which is not chicken feed.
On a user pay-back basis.

Motion No. 7
That Bill C-92, to amend the National Harbours Board Act, the Government Harbours and Piers Act, the Harbour Commissions Act, the Canada Shipping Act and the Fishing and Recreational Harbours Act, be amended in Clause 14 by striking out line 14 at page 23 and substituting the following therefor:
"cases.
40. The Minister, the Corporation or a local port corporation shall not, by virtue of anything provided by or under this Act, be deemed to have the administration, management or control of any scheduled harbour as defined in section 2 of the Fishing and Recreational Harbours Act." "
He said: Mr. Speaker, 1 will abbreviate my explanation of this motion. Clause 7 of the bill as printed provides:
"9. (1) The Governor in Council may, by order, at any time, on the recommendation of the Minister,
(a)	transfer to the Corporation for administration, management and control
any harbour, work or property of Canada-
That clause provides a substantial expropriation power to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to enlarge the boundaries and jurisdiction of the Canada Ports Corporation to encompass other ports which are owned by Her Majesty and operated in the name of the Government of Canada. I had hoped-this is reflected in a motion printed on the Order Paper last week-to find a way to exempt harbours that are operating under the Harbour Commissions Act or the Government Harbours and Piers Act, former acts governing the management of these other types of harbours owned by Her Majesty, from any overriding power or expropriation threat by the provisions of Bill C-92. I have been led to believe that the government will find the present motion acceptable. It would exempt harbours operating under the provisions of small craft harbours legislation from any possible threat of expropriation by way of enlarging the head line of ports operated by the Canada Ports Corporation. I only regret that the minister had not seen fit also to provide similar guarantees to protect harbour commission ports because, as we determined through our long committee deliberations, it has been an objective from the outset that if a local port corporation sought to establish harbour commission status or Class D Crown corporation status, that would be permitted. I am afraid that, given the very powerful expropriation provision in Clause 7(9) the minister, in his judgment, could at some time in the future reacquire a harbour commission port and take it into the family of ports operating under the Canada Ports Corporation.
Be that as it may, Mr. Speaker, I am led to believe that the government will find this amendment acceptable. It will protect all the small craft harbours in Canada, including the
Canada Ports Corporation Act
two in my riding, at Ladner and Steveston, from possible acquisition by the Canada Ports Corporation.

Mr. Speaker, the purpose of the amendment is to establish symmetry between the Fishing and Recreational Harbours Act and the Canada Ports Corporation Act so that one cannot infringe upon the other. It is a search for symmetry and we thought it was implied in the spirit of the bill. If my hon. friend wants to spell it out, that is all right.

Motion No. 8
That Bill C-92, An Act to amend the National Harbours Board Act, the Government Harbours and Piers Act, the Harbour Commissions Act, the Canada Shipping Act and the Fishing and Recreational Harbours Act, be amended in Clause 15 by striking out lines 20 to 28 at page 23 and substituting the following therefor:
"chairman, a vice-chairman and five other directors.
2.(1) Subject to this section, three of the directors of a local port corporation
shall be appointed by the Governor in Council and the remainder shall be
appointed by the Governor in Council based on recommendations as follows:
(a)	one by the Lieutenant Governor in Council of the province in which the local port corporation is located;
(b)	one director by agreement among the councils of all municipalities adjoining the port for which the local port corporation is established;
(c)	one by the provincial federation of labour in consultation with the marine and maritime unions; and
{d) one by the agreement of the commercial tenants of the local port corporation."
She said: Mr. Speaker, I should like to refer to this motion so that we know the context in which we are discussing it. In our view this is probably the most important amendment to the bill. Unless we can have the whole concept of local autonomy included in port management, it means nothing. There must be a board that is accountable to the local community as well as able to carry out the responsibility of the national port objectives. We believe it is very important to have a local board for local port corporations. It is important that we not have a

July 26, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
patronage board, as was mentioned by a member from Newfoundland, but a sound, democratic board that will be efficient and have expertise in a number of areas.
Our amendment proposes a seven-person board composed of a chairman, a vice-chairperson and five directors. Three of the directors would be appointed by the federal government and, in addition, four members would be appointed by the minister, but the four names could be submitted in four different areas of interest. We feel, for example, that the government of the province in which the port is located should be able to propose one or more names to the minister representing the regional planning interests, the industrial and economic development interests which are of major concern to the province. In a province with coastal regions, the total industry of the province is tied into the port system, so it only makes sense that it should have some say in appointments to the board.
We also propose that municipalities surrounding the particular port should have the right to propose names to the minister. Several names could be suggested of persons expert in port and regional matters and the concerns of the municipalities-not in a vested interest way, because they would represent all municipalities, but in a practical, planning way. They would know the environmental and other concerns of the surrounding municipalities.
We also propose that port users-domestic port users, should be able to name nominees for the consideration of the minister; perhaps one representative from that group. Surely the users of the port should have a voice. They would have a certain expertise to contribute to the board. We also propose a representative from labour-not a representative of one particular union but a representative of labour generally. Names could be submitted through the Canadian Federation of Labour in consultation with the marine unions.
This seemed to us to be a way of conforming to certain structures that are required for Crown corporations but still achieving a balanced approach to the composition of local port boards.
1 should like to refer to the objectives that were established and that have been spoken to already. How can we possibly achieve Canadian international trade objectives and represent the concerns of all provinces using a port unless one member of the board has this kind of expertise? In the port of Vancouver, for example, I could see the need for someone tied in with the prairie provinces, with the lumber industry-someone who is knowledgeable about the Pacific rim trade interests.
In our objectives we said that there should be efficiency. That is one criteria of a sound local port corporations policy. This means there should be members on the board with business expertise. We know that the minister will think of these people first. In committee he automatically thought of the chamber of commerce, as did the Conservative Party which would automatically go to that group first. That is fine, let us have a member from the chamber of commerce, but let us also have persons expert in labour relations or who have knowledge of transportation or shipping and of the problems of dock workers.
We said in our objectives that there should be equitable treatment, in the movement of goods and persons, of users of the port. Domestic users should have a voice on the board. They could make a valuable contribution, speaking for all users of the port and for the business community, providing useful advice for policy making as well as the day-to-day operations of the port.
We said in our objectives that the port policy should provide local port corporations with a high degree of autonomy for management and operation of the port. It seems to me just common sense that persons nominated for the board should include some who know something about the surrounding municipalities and communities, as well as the provincial economic development concerns. The official opposition stated in one of its amendments, and we agree, that these should not be elected politicians but persons who have expertise in port matters and in planning in the areas I have mentioned.
It is important that there be co-ordination with other marine activities and with multi-mode types of transportation.
This would no be political patronage of appointees made by the minister in the typical Liberal way that we want. If we are to have autonomy in the local port corporations, the boards must have a broad composition with input from the groups that I have described.
We feel that the process of appointment to the board could be carried out through a procedure that would allow the minister to name the appointees. The minister did not seem to comprehend this is committee. I understand this idea was taken to cabinet and vetoed there. That is not an unexpected action by a Liberal cabinet, of course. The minister would still have certain veto rights, as would cabinet, but he would be able to choose three of the appointees in addition to the four groups that 1 have mentioned.
I do not really grasp the rationale of his argument when he said that special interests would dominate this kind of board structure. If ever we had special interests, it is under the present and proposed situation where the minister will appoint all the representatives to the board. Why does he think that one provincial representative, for example, would be able to out-vote six others? That is not special interest, that is just one out of seven who would express an interest that the province might have but who would be concerned as well with the port operation generally. The same thing applies to labour. The minister has given lip service to labour in that two local port authorities of the NHB have labour representatives, but there is no assurance that this would be part of the regular structure. If he agrees with it for two local port authorities, why could he not put it in writing as the criterion for the appointment of all boards across the country?
I was interested in a number of amendments proposed by the Conservatives, and we did agree with some of them as I said earlier. We believe the local port board, for example, should be able to elect its own chairperson. Why should that have to be done by the minister and approved by cabinet? In
July 26, 1982

addition, surely a local board would be responsible and competent enough to nominate replacements and have them approved by the minister on their recommendation. It is interesting to note that the Conservatives proposed a system similar to the Harbours Commission when they were talking about the composition of the local advisory board. They wanted to have municipal representation, but I did not see it stated anywhere in their amendments that the province should have the right to some representation on the local board. I was very interested in that inasmuch as it was the hon. member for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook) who pressed very hard in committee to have witnesses come forward. We received a telegram from the Government of British Columbia saying that they do not agree with this bill at all and they wanted to have a B.C. port authority, a whole new authority for the province. We do not agree with that but 1 think it would make great sense to have the provinces, particularly in the larger ports, have a say and be able to propose at least one person to the board. I was curious as to why the Conservatives did not include this in their amendment.
In the case of the refusal by the minister and the government to consider our amendment, or even to modify it, I can only conclude that it confirms our major concern that the Liberal government still wants to maintain patronage appointments to these new local port boards. If this is the case- certainly there is nothing to indicate that it is not-it seems to me that it undermines the whole concept of autonomy, supposedly the main purpose of this bill. We know the appointees are going to be friends of the Liberals, if not actual party members. We have heard about former Liberal candidates appointed to boards under the present system. As soon as you get a board which is largely a patronage type of board, we will also have them deciding on leases. Certainly a lot of us have concerns about how leases are approved and about the granting of important financial advantages to persons receiving leases of port property.
I do not want to take any more time on this amendment, Mr. Speaker, but it is really a very important one, and 1 wish the minister would reconsider. I believe that in principle the opposition parties supported this in committee as well, and unless there is a more sound and representative local port board the proposed autonomy will simply not take place.

Mr. Speaker, just a few brief comments in connection with this particular amendment. It deals basically with the same material for which my party fought very hard in committee and in bargaining with the parliamentary secretary to get some kind of amendment of this nature. I mention in passing that this is not unique. The government will obviously turn down this amendment, not that the minister is opposed that much to it but because his cabinet colleagues booted him out of the room when he tried to suggest it might be reasonable to allow various ports to nominate two or three people from various segments of the population involved with that port. He would then still have the option of making his selection from that group. The minister, of course, was personally totally opposed to having any provincial input, and in the hopes of getting
Canada Ports Corporation Act
something through which might make sense we dropped it from our amendment. Finally, when we realized the hopelessness of the whole thing, we withdrew our amendment.
I am delighted to see that the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) has at least brought this to the attention of the House, even though it was a futile effort. I support this amendment, and I would support a far better one, but seeing that it is not going to happen anyway I would only warn the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, that his appointments to local port corporations and the Canada Ports Corporation are going to be watched very carefully by all port people throughout Canada. The minister is going to be watched very carefully to see whether he has gone the usual Liberal route of pure patronage, or whether he has attempted to find people from the port community, the labour unions or the municipalities, in other words, whether there is a balanced board and one that knows its stuff, or whether it is going to be another group of Liberal party hacks. Rest assured, Sir, that I will be the first one screaming if you appoint the kind of board which you have the absolute dictatorial power to do. That is what we are objecting to and that is why we want this type of amendment. I compliment the hon. member for Vancouver East on bringing this forward so that it can be discussed, at least very briefly.

Mr. Speaker, my remarks will be short because many of us will not be speaking on third reading if things go as it appears they will this evening.
One of the two very strongly held concerns of members of this party is with respect to providing local autonomy. The other concern has to do with providing a degree of financial independence to the local port corporation, and the minister has graciously accommodated that. I would go so far as to say, Mr. Speaker, that if the minister were prepared to accept at least an undertaking to consult with the regional advisory council, which he will appoint under the provisions of this bill and which was the nature of amendments presented in committee and in fact listed on the Order Paper last week, then I could support this bill, even though I am not terribly happy about creating another family of Crown corporations. I am sure other members may feel that way also because it is like a slap in the face to our constituents to see rehashed, retired or defeated liberal candidates appointed to responsible positions. I recall asking the administrator in committee how these lists were prepared. Was it at departmental level and sent to the minister for selection and decision, or were the lists submitted to the administrator by the political structure for comment? I could gauge by the twindle in the administrator's eye that it was the latter course which was followed. I must say that is a sad commentary on the way we select people for responsible positions where they are entrusted with policy decisions and the over-all management of major Crown corporations such as the proposed Canada Ports Corporation. I cannot support the bill as written, largely because of this remaining deficiency which I would like to have seen rectified. I hope in these final moments the minister might agree to accept the amendment

July 26, 1982
Canada Ports Corporation Act
proposed by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell). It reflects the concerns of the people in my province and of the government of British Columbia to some degree because they have made it quite clear that they cannot accept the bill in its present form.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a few comments so that it will not be said that I did not answer the last question. With respect to Motion No. 8, I disagree with the principle that is introduced which is group representation as opposed to representation by individuals. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) gave us four groups that she would like to see represented: the provinces, the municipalities, labour and tenants. I could name other groups. For instance users-
I said users.

-carriers, women, academics and environmental groups. Immediately you have a problem having to decide which groups are going to be selected. There are ten or 15 different groups that can relate to the objectives of a port. I have answered questions in committee as to provincial representation in these matters. But I should underline the fact that there is a new element in that bill. It sets the qualifications of those who will become members of the board. Proven experience and capacity is one of the criteria. As a member said, they have to know their stuff, which is one of the conditions for appointment. They have to be representative of local interests. Generally they have to have residence in the area of the port itself.
In committee I said that I would be looking forward to recommendations and suggestions made by different groups in society. I do not think it would be wise to appoint people to these boards on the basis that they represent this or that particular group.
