Mr. Speaker, I have spent a good many years of my life on this bill. I want to take a few miniutes to speak briefly on third reading. I could discuss many of the claims made in committee and here today but I will resist that temptation. Simply in my opinion, this bill is long past due. It has the support of the vast majority of the people involved in the ports community of Canada. A fair number of amendments have been accepted by the government, some of which in my own opinion make the bill weaker and some make it stronger, but that is the nature of the give and take and compromise of debate.
I believe it is now time to get on with Bill C-92 as amended and have passage of it today. I want to pay tribute to the committee, of which I had the honour to be chairman, for the diligence and the hard work which its member showed. There was a fair amount of partisanship, which one expected in a parliamentary democracy, but there was a maximum sense of public duty displayed by members who served on that committee.
I would like to pay particular tribute to the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) who is probably more knowledgeable than any other member in this House on ports policy in Canada. I want to pay tribute also to the member for Laprairie (Mr. Deniger). He was the ViceChairman of the committee. He chaired several sessions of the committee in my absence due to the death of a member of my family. In addition, I want to pay tribute to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, the hon. member for Parkdale-High Park (Mr. Flis) for his diligence in ensuring that we were all well-informed on the various points in the bill.
The minister attended the committee and gave full and frank answers to the questions presented to him. Finally, I would like to mention the administrator of the Canadian Marine Transportation Administration who spent quite some time in the committee. He was the chief witness. He, with his officials, deserve the commendation of the committee and the gratitude of the people of Canada for the fine job they are doing in administering the marine division.
July 26, 1982

Having said that, I express the hope that this bill will pass without further delay and that we will have in this country not independent ports but autonomous ports still responsible to the Government of Canada for their actions and, through the Government of Canada, to the people of Canada. I hope that we will have a very healthy and active port community as a result of the passage of Bill C-92 as amended.

Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief. It has taken a long time to push this bill through. I think everyone who served on the committee worked very hard.
I want to state flatly and get it on the record that I will be voting against this bill. I shall be saying no to this bill because of the absolute powers it gives to the minister in practically everything. Perhaps I am wrong. Perhaps I am wrong to distrust a Liberal government that has been riddled with patronage of various kinds. Perhaps I am wrong to distrust civil servants in Ottawa for fear of what they may do in terms of continuing to attempt to run anything out of this centre which is 4,000 miles from my port.
If we can believe what the minister says and if we can believe what the administrator has had to say this bill may work out. But every time I look at the actual document and I try to find where it is written that we have autonomy, I cannot because it is simply not there.
I warned my colleagues and the port users of Vancouver about this bill. Never has there been a time when a member representing the west coast hoped that he was wrong about a bill in Parliament. If I am wrong I will be delighted. If I am right, then this is a terrible bill. One of the first things we will do when we take over the government will be to change this legislation, if the minister uses his autocratic powers and if the minister handles the bill with the vast powers he has. I only hope that I am wrong. But for the record I say that I will be voting a strong and vehement no to this dictatorial piece of legislation with regard to the ports of Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jesse P. Flis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one of the main objectives of-the national ports policy for Canada is to create a port system that is an effective instrument of support for the achievement of Canadian international trade objectives.
Canada is an active trading partner ranking eighth internationally in terms of the value of our exports. Merchandise exports are 25 per cent of our gross national product while our total external trade accounts for nearly one third of our GNP.
In the midst of today's world recession, competition for exports has become a battleground for economic survival. International competition in this environment of uncertainty will test severely Canada's ability to enhance or even maintain its existing trade position. As the battle for world trade advantage becomes fiercer, Canada must strive to have the best ports facilities in the world. Efficient ports can reduce the cost of our products significantly, making them more competitive on world markets.
Canada Ports Corporation Act
The ports policy which we are shaping in the House today must be sensitive and respond to changing trade patterns. For example, three years ago, for the first time, our trade across the Pacific exceeded that across the Atlantic. Export market opportunities are shifting away from North America and Europe to Southeast Asia, the Middle East and Latin America.
Last year the special parliamentary committee on a national trading corporation tabled in the House a report entitled, "Canada's Trade Challenge". The bill we are about to pass this evening will provide a very important component in helping Canadians meet Canada's trade challenge.
It became evident 12 years ago that Canada's ports policy was no longer adequate to meet the economic and social needs of the eighties and nineties. Attempts to change the existing legislation to make it more responsive in meeting the needs for greater local and regional involvement in the operations and development of the ports within the NHB system failed.
A special task force of industry representatives and government was formed eight years ago to review Canadian ports policy and make recommendations on changes. The task force laid the foundation of a new policy by developing a series of objectives for the ports system. These objectives are clearly spelled out in Clause 2, subclause 3(1) of the bill. Therefore I will not waste the time of the House by reading the objectives. Taking into account the task force recommendations, new legislation was prepared and brought before the chamber in 1977 as Bill C-61, then again in the same year as Bill C-6, and two years later as Bill C-50. All three bills died on the Order Paper without even reaching second reading.
After being three times a bridesmaid, it is time that Bill C-92 became a bride, led to the altar by the distinguished groom, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). This bride, Bill C-92, is being given away tonight by her father, the administrator of Canadian marine transport administration, Mr. Gordon Sinclair.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
If anyone deserves to claim the title of father of Bill C-92, the administrator certainly does. His many consultations with all interested parties across Canada on this bill, his information, advice and answers in committee, and his unlimited patience went a long way in bringing Bill C-92 to report stage.
In every wedding party there must be a best man. I would like to bestow this honour upon the chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport. Bill C-92 could have received the same ill fate as past ports bills, but thanks to his fairness to every committee member, regardless of party affiliation, the bill received careful scrutiny and came out of committee a better bill.
As Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, I want to thank the ushers of this wedding party-the hon. members for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall), for
19716

Canada Ports Corporation Act
Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), for North Vancouver-Burnaby (Mr. Cook), for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon), for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain), and others from the Official Opposition whose questions, clarifications and amendments have brought more clarity and strength to Bill C-92.
Of course, what would we have done without the bridesmaids? The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) kept reminding the committee that there were two sexes in the world. She and her colleague, the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) stressed the importance of more decentralized administration-
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. 1 hate to take the time of the House, but I really object to the language just used by the parliamentary secretary.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry the hon. member objects to those words. I thought I was complimenting the hon. member. If she thinks they are offensive, I will withdraw them.
Also I would like to throw orchids to the hon. members of the Standing Committee on Transport from this side of the House for their dedication in attending committee meetings and for their defence of the bill. I must congratulate them for even voting against the government and with the opposition to pass the opposition motion on the appointment of auditors by local boards.
To complete the wedding party on this bill, I know that all hon. members of the House who served on the transport committee would want me to congratulate the mother of the bride, the clerk of the transport committee, Miss Santosh Sirpaul who was so helpful to all committee members in making certain that our amendments were in order and that the committee proceedings flowed as smoothly as possible.
After 12 years of attempts to improve our ports legislation, I am pleased and indeed honoured that I find myself standing in the House of Commons in the midst of parliamentarians who are providing outstanding leadership today for a better Canada tomorrow.

We were going to support the bill until we heard
that speech.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague says that we were going to support the bill until we heard that speech. That is not true. We are not going to support the bill. We agree that Bill C-92 is long overdue. In my remarks on June 22 I reviewed the history of the many attempts from 1901 on to establish more local autonomy and more efficiency in the ports system.
The ports policy of Canada is basic to our economic development and to our international trade. It creates jobs. It is essential to industrial development. It affects the quality of our life. Indeed, it is very, very important to all regions of Canada which are located on the waters of our continent. We believe that the ports policy must be efficient and decentralized to reflect regional needs.
The aim of Bill C-92 was to establish local autonomy. We think it has provided more local decentralized administration.
July 26, 1982
There is more control over funds, particularly since the amendment passed today. However, we are not satisfied at all that there really is local autonomy in the true sense of the word. In particular, we are concerned that the board of directors of local port organizations will still be appointed by the minister. It is not a democratic board. There is no assurance that the objectives of Bill C-92 will be carried out because of it.
We in this party believe very strongly that we must also maintain a national ports policy which takes into consideration the needs of all regions-the prairies, to get their grain to port; northern areas, to get lumber and similar resources to port. We must be concerned about smaller ports which may need more federal support in the form of subsidies. Therefore we are concerned that this bill requires financial independence for a port to qualify to have local autonomy. Specifically we agree with the provision of regional advisory councils. It is a good move. It does not establish an authority at the provincial level, but we believe that it provides for the kind of planning that is needed.
There are positives in this bill, but unfortunately the negatives remain and are serious. Our amendment to link a Canadian marines strategy with the objectives was refused. The user-pay policy for ports which has now been established by the Liberals will be implicit in this policy. It could destroy some of the ports which are not able to be financially self-sufficient, and require them to charge fuller fees so that they would not be competitive and might lose customers.
Debts have been written off at this time, but there is no assurance in the future that there will not be ports operating in the red which will need help. Finally, we feel that the local autonomy is tokenism as long as there is central control in Ottawa. We agree with some of our colleagues to the right that there are many things in the bill which appear to be decentralized, but ultimately the control is in the hands of the minister and ultimately in the hands of cabinet.
I join in thanking all hon. members who participated in committee. I commend, particularly, the staff who spent many long hours and were most efficient in performing their duties.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I hesitate to rise because it is now ten o'clock, but having remained silent all day in spite of many things, there are two comments which could be made, one of which I make without any hesitation whatsoever. There is no parent, no bride and no bridegroom in this. I agree with my colleague from Vancouver East (Mrs. Mitchell) that the sexism in this bill should disappear. However, that is another matter altogether.
If there is a real parentage to this that will measure up to his work and those who put together the National Harbours Board some 45 or 46 years ago, perhaps it is the process, because the process has been seen to work. In many respects I agree with
July 26, 1982

the forcefulness of the representations by my colleagues from Vancouver, and in some respects I disagree with them.
This is a bill that I can support and I agree that the port users in this country by and large can support it. It is a bill that I hope will serve our ports and serve the objectives that have been outlined by a variety of members under different guises and different amendments throughout today. I hope that the bill does in fact serve those ends. Autonomy is something that we can achieve.
When the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) was minister of transport, I believe he was bent in that direction. 1 pay some tribute to him for having brought the bill to its present state. Had the government moved with respect to Crown corporations, given an indication of where it was going in that area, a lot of the difficulty surrounding this bill might have been shortcircuited. On the other hand, I can only say to the House, to the minister and the marine administrator and his staff that 1 appreciate their tolerance, understanding and patience. I hope the work they have done in terms of passage of this bill to serve the needs of our importers and exporters is in fact there and can meet the challenge that lies in front of us. I appreciate having had the opportunity to be part of the debate which is now some 10 or 12 years old.

subtopic: MINES AND MINING-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE. (B) LABOUR RELATIONS
MINES AND MINING-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE. (B) LABOUR RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 2, 1982, as recorded at page 18018 of Hansard, 1 directed questions to the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the absence of the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) relating to the serious and growing crisis of employment in Canada's mining industry. At that time I pointed out that the current inventory as of early June showed that more than 34,000 mine, mill and smelter workers would be unemployed this summer largely because of announced shut-downs and work curtailments which were announced through the early part of this year.
I point out that if we take into account the multiplier effect to the people in all of these very seriously impacted mining communities across Canada, the people whose livelihood is directly related to the mining industry, we would find more than 160,000 employees across Canada, mostly in towns that are very heavily dependent upon single industries, who will see a major portion of their income impaired for 1982. I asked the Prime Minister to tell us what specific initiatives the government was preparing to take in the face of this serious dilemma and, in fact, what recommendations the hon. Minister of State for Mines had presented to cabinet in order to provide some hope of recovery to Canada's mining industry in the months ahead.
It has often been said that the plight of the industry has resulted from international factors and circumstances. I want to take a few moments tonight to point out that many sectors of our mining industry in Canada are in very seriously devastating circumstances because of domestic factors which cannot be entirely ascribed to international conditions.
Let me refer to a speech by the incoming president of the Mining Association of Canada in late May, who said that the problem of the Canadian minerals industry is not that of a lack of demand for Canadian minerals in foreign markets. He said that the problem is essentially domestic. 1 would put a lot of credibility in such words from the new president of the mining association. He went on to say that what is needed is determination by the government to restore an environment that encourages mineral development in Canada.
If we look at other observations on the discussion paper put forward by the Minister of State for Mines a few months ago, particularly if we look at the reaction of the Mining Association of Canada under the signature of David Thomas, the previous president, who wrote to the minister on May 29,

July 26, 1982
Adjournment Debate
1982, we find that there is great alarm about the lopsided inferences on social priorities and the lack of recognition of the serious structural inadequacies in our taxation policy with respect to mining investment and development. Mr. Thomas also pointed out the regrettable fact, and I refer to his letter to the minister, that over the past few years Canada's share of the world market has not been maintained and it should be recognized that if slippage has occurred, it is due not only to changing international conditions of supply and demand of minerals, but also, in no small extent, to the fact that investor confidence in mineral development in Canada stagnated during the seventies as a result of taxation and disputes between the two levels of Canadian government and other related factors.
Since I asked these questions in the House of Commons on June 2, the situation has grown worse. If we do our sums now, we find something in excess of 42,000 mine workers stand to be unemployed by the end of this summer. We should consider that the current serious economic depression really did not gain momentum until after the Easter period. We are now to be forewarned that the lay-offs which were only to cover a period of six weeks or eight weeks through the summer months are now being extended.
If we read the headlines we see, for example, that Cyprus Anvil in the Yukon is in serious trouble, affecting some 1,000 miners and over 40 per cent of the Yukon economy. These unemployed miners are likely to remain unemployed through the winter months if the federal government does not take some action soon. Another headline states, that The NorthWest Territories exploration activity is down substantially. Another headline is to the effect that the potash mine reopenings are still in doubt. Another headline is to the effect that Hudsons Bay Mining is extending its shutdown and smelter workers may lose their jobs if the strike continues. Another one is to the effect that the investment lull could debilitate the economy well into 1984. Another is to the effect that Inco would reinstitute production halts even if workers returned, and they have returned. Another one states that Ontario uranium mines have shut down.
In conclusion, I would like to say that one of the most seriously impacted areas of our mining industry in northern Ontario is the Timiskaming area, where we have three mines, the Adams mine, the Griffiths mine and the Sherman mine, all supplying the total production to the Canadian steel industry. The other day we learned about the very unfortunate collapse or shutdown of the Defasco mill in Hamilton. The Stelco mill is also supplied from the Adams mine, and we have the serious problems involving the collapse of the northern gas pipeline, and Algoma Steel, which is cutting back severely on its demand for iron ore pellets. We should recognize that the iron ore economy of northern Ontario, in Kirkland Lake and in other areas in the Timiskaming region, is entirely dependent on iron ore production and that, in fact, the downturn is largely due to domestic factors and we cannot blame the world. We must blame the policies, the budgetary initiatives of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the government opposite. I would be very pleased to hear the Minister of State for Mines deny that that is the case.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MINES AND MINING-REQUEST FOR ASSISTANCE. (B) LABOUR RELATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to reply to the statements by the hon. member for Richmond-South Delta (Mr. Siddon) on the state of the Canadian mining industry. I only wish I had the next 40 minutes to tell him exactly how this government is responding. Unfortunately, I do not.
Since he has painted such a picture of doom and gloom, I believe it is my responsibility to point out to him some of the bright spots that are occurring in Canada. I refer him to the most recent issue of The Northern Miner which states that the Canadian uranium outsells others in the United States market. Canadian producers are winning a large share of the current United States demand for long-term or large quantity uranium contracts.
It goes on to say that during the first six months of this year several major reported sales contracts involved approximately 30 million pounds of uranium. Just over half of the contract, or approximately 15 million pounds, went to non-U.S. companies for uranium to be produced in Canada. The willingness to adjust to the realities of the market is the primary reason that Canadian sellers have been so successful in obtaining new sales commitments.
I would have the hon. member know that the uranium mines in northern Ontario are running at full production. I also refer him to another rather successful spot in the Canadian mining scene, and I refer to the statement that gold keeps glister for Quebec mines.
Let me refer to The Financial Post, which states that the long established gold mining industry of northwestern Quebec centred in this town, aptly named Valley of Gold, is reasonably stable despite the fall in gold prices. This 70-mile wide stretch of the Canadian shield accounts for about one-third of the country's gold production worth about $230 million a year at recent prices and keeps as many as 8,000 people employed directly and indirectly.
It goes on to say that of the ten operating mines visited recently, all but one are making cash profits at the mine site, in some cases quite handsome profits. These ten mines appear more than capable of producing about 520,000 ounces of gold this year, and they employ about 2,000 at their operation, and that is not counting the spin-off that mining generates in services, supplies and transportation industries, creating perhaps another 6,000 jobs. All is not doom and gloom. I would go on to say that the hon. member well knows and refuses to admit that the vast majority of lay-offs in the country is due to a worldwide recession.
He asks, and I am sorry my time is limited, what we are doing. We know how bad the situation is in some areas. Therefore we have in place safety nets such as the Unemployment Insurance Act to maintain income and keep the economy of the community reasonably stable. God knows we are grateful for it, particularly in the area from which I come. We
July 26, 1982

have, under Section 38, created quite a number of jobs. I suggest to the hon. member that he look at what has happened under Section 38.
I also suggest to the hon. member that he take his duties more seriously, as have some members of the New Democratic Party. They have taken the time to come to us to see just how Section 38 can be applied to those areas of the country from which they come. They are now making an intensive effort to see that it works so that miners who are skilled will retain their skills, their dignity and have a decent income to bring home to their families. I suggest to him that he have another look. He derides and laughs at Section 38. 1 suggest to him that those very mining companies and the presidents to whom he referred as not having much faith in which is happening are the very ones who have been sitting down at the table with me to make it happen. Therefore, 1 say to him that this government is very concerned and acting very decisively to make things happen in these mining communities.

subtopic: EXPORT DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-FUNDS LENT TO NEW YORK METROPOLITAN TRANSPORTATION AUTHORITY
EXPORT DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION-FUNDS LENT TO NEW YORK METROPOLITAN TRANSPORTATION AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question 1 would like to have debated this evening arises from the deal signed between the government, through its agency, the Export Development Corporation, and the New York Transit Authority, wherein it is contemplated that over the next 15 years the Government of Canada, through that agency, EDC, will be financing the purchase of certain transit equipment for the city of New York. This will require total borrowing on the part of the Government of Canada of $563 million over 15 years, with a rate of interest of only 9.7 per cent as far as New York is concerned.
.
If I may, I would like to clarify that because most people can hardly believe we have a government that is so careless and so reckless with its financing for foreign entities that it would literally borrow money at a true cost of 16 per cent today and lend it to an agency such as the New York Transit Authority at 9.7 per cent.
When this deal was announced, the officials with the New York Transit Authority could not believe their good fortune. They could not believe there was a Santa Claus north of the border, in the form of the Government of Canada, which was willing to make a gift to them-it was not even Christmas at the time-of $300 million to be spread over the next 15 years. That is the hard-earned money of Canadians which is being routed by this government into the development of a transit system for the benefit of those who happen to live in New York.
The hon. member for Mississauga North (Mr. Fisher) is in the House this evening. I wish he would familiarize his constituents with the fact that while some of them are losing their homes as a result of 18 per cent, 19 per cent and 20 per cent financing, his government, which triggered the high interest
Adjournment Debate
structure in the country to begin with, has now found money to lend to the New York Transit Authority at 9.7 per cent.
The government alleges it will create 20,000 to 25,000 jobs, but let us bear in mind that those 20,000 to 25,000 jobs will be spread over five years, so that in total there will only be 5,000 jobs created per year. However, we then take a new look and find that 40 per cent of the jobs will be created in the United States, so the net number of Canadians who will be employed in an area where unemployment is very high, Quebec, is only 3,000 per year. Translated into job costs per year, that means it will cost the Canadian public $20,000 in interest costs alone to keep those 3,000 employees employed over the next five years.
That is only part of the problem. In making this move, I would say that the government has acted in open defiance of the agreement, to which it is a party, with the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development group of nations in which it was agreed that in future export credits would be limited so that rates would never go below 11.25 per cent. A recent agreement raised that to 12.5 per cent. In any event, it was agreed that in no event would there be loans to support exports of longer than eight and a half years. The government not only is favouring a foreign entity at the expense of Canadians but also violating the very OECD agreement to which it is a party.
If there is this money available to build transit equipment and services for foreign entities, why is it not available in Canada? Why does the Toronto transit authority not have access to 9.7 per cent money if it should decide-which it would love to do-to extend the subway system in Toronto? What about Montreal? Why are the people of Montreal second-class citizens in relation to those in New York? What about Vancouver, Edmonton, Calgary or any other major urban area? And what about Ottawa? What is wrong with the citizens of these communities that this government, which loves to talk pompously about its resistance to Americanism, should turn around and favour a city like New York at the expense of comparable cities in Canada?
Is it Canadian technology we are talking about in relation to this wonderful coup-this wonderful contract-the government claims it has got itself into? No, it is Japanese technology. The research and development and the design of this equipment was all done on a licence from Japanese concerns. Not even there do we get any distinct benefit from this billion dollar financing-when interest is included-that the government has committed us to.
We could ask the government's spokesperson, whoever that is-I notice there is only one member left in the House to defend the government-if he was ever consulted about this contract before it was entered into. Was it ever made known to the various poor, unfortunate wretches who happen to be Liberal MPs from the Toronto area, that this is the type of shenanigan the government they so loyally support, intended to get into at the expense of millions of Canadian taxpayers?

Adjournment Debate
At a time when we are facing an estimated deficit of some $25 billion due to mismanagement by the government-a deficit that is, in relative terms, greater than that of any other industrialized nation in the world-the government is not out finding money at 9.7 per cent in order to help the residents of Toronto, Montreal, Vancouver, Edmonton, Calgary, Winnipeg, Ottawa or wherever you like, but is finding 9.7 per cent money to help the residents of New York. Surely some explanation is due, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-STATUS OF NATIVE WOMEN- ATTENDANCE AT CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE. (B) REQUEST THAT NATIVE WOMEN BE REPRESENTED
THE CONSTITUTION-STATUS OF NATIVE WOMEN- ATTENDANCE AT CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE. (B) REQUEST THAT NATIVE WOMEN BE REPRESENTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 16 I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) if he would invite representatives of the Native Women's Association of Canada to attend the coming constitutional conference. Because of the long-standing discrimination under the Indian Act against Indian women it is important that they should have direct representation at the conference when it deals with constitutional matters directly affecting aboriginal peoples. In response the Prime Minister said he was inviting representatives of the three national organizations representing the Indian, Inuit and Metis people. He tried to make the case that somehow I was uncomplimentary to these organizations when I said they all had their own legitimate concerns, in pursuit of which the unique problems of Indian women could very easily be overlooked.
The Indian people as a whole, Mr. Speaker, and in particular their leaders, are very nervous about the outcome of the constitutional conference. They are anxious about their rights and what might happen when the federal and provincial governments sit down to horse trade. I believe they have good reason to be concerned, although I still hope the outcome of the talks might be a very positive definition of aboriginal and treaty rights. The struggle to gain that definition will take all the time and energy of these organizations, and it is not insult to say that in doing so the three national organizations 1 mentioned will not give top priority to solving the problems of Indian women. The fact is that male Indian leaders are no better and no worse at representing women than other male leaders. However, the record of other male leaders in our society has not been good.
This past spring all women in Canada were shocked when they saw how some male parliamentarians joked about the question of violence against women. Many of them remember the shameful way in which the first ministers of the provinces, meeting with the Prime Minister last fall, jetisoned their rights in the constitutional accord. The first ministers threw women's guarantees of equality overboard at the same time as they ditched aboriginal rights. The rights of women and the rights of aboriginal people were discarded as being inconsequential. When we look at the record of some of the male Indian leaders we see that some are very supportive of Indian women and others are not.
But I ask what reason do Indian women have for confidence in the next first ministers' conference unless they have direct representation? As of this spring the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) indicated he had not even begun to sit down with the leaders of the Indian people to discuss how discrimination could be ended. It is true
July 26, 1982

that within three years the new Charter of Rights and Freedoms will not allow the discrimination involved in Section 12(1 )(b) of the Indian Act; that is, unless Section 33 of the Constitution Act is invoked and the government passed a bill saying that Section 12(1 )(b) of the Indian Act applied notwithstanding the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. But even when Section 12(l)(b) of the Indian Act is declared unconstitutional, there is still the question of retroactivity. How are we going to do justice to the hundreds of Indian women and to their children who have already lost their status? There is a great need for all parties to this question-the federal government, the provinces, the Indian organizations and organizations representing Indian women-to sit down at a conference table and thresh out this problem to avoid a hasty or inadequate solution.
A cabinet document dated September 28, 1981, estimated the cost of reinstatement of women who have already lost their status to be in the neighborhood of half a billion dollars, in order that the re-entry of these women into Indian bands would not further impoverish those bands. In addition, there would have to be a program of land entitlement so that population pressures on the land base would not become worse than they already are.
Obviously the government sees some very important federal-provincial implications in this issue. If the matter is going to be discussed at a federal-provincial forum, Indian women should be directly involved. The Native Women's Association of Canada has a mandate to represent Indian, Metis and Inuit women from across Canada. Considering the history of discrimination Indian women have faced, they need to be represented directly at the first ministers' conference. Again I appeal to the government to invite representatives of the Native Women's Association of Canada to sit at that table, and I ask the parliamentary secretary if the government is willing to do so.

speakeroldname: Mr. Douglas Fisher (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE CONSTITUTION-STATUS OF NATIVE WOMEN- ATTENDANCE AT CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE. (B) REQUEST THAT NATIVE WOMEN BE REPRESENTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a real pleasure to be able to take part in this debate with the hon. member and to provide him with some extra information. I know his concern about this issue is genuine, and I congratulate him for the effort and conscience he has used to bring this issue forward.
Adjournment Debate
Since funding to national and territorial organizations of aboriginal people began in 1980, the federal government has urged these organizations to develop more explicit positions with respect to constitutional issues of particular interest to aboriginal women.
On June 16 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated in this House that he would see whether aboriginal groups would have any suggestions regarding the representation of aboriginal women at the upcoming conference of First ministers on the Constitution. On June 22 the Prime Minister met with representatives of the three national aboriginal organizations. He was informed by one of the co-chair persons of the Inuit Committee on National Issues that their organization would be prepared to allow a spokesperson for aboriginal women to occupy, for part of the conference, one of the seats allocated to represent natives of the Inuit Committee on National Issues. This is a progressive step and hopefully one which will be followed by the Native Council of Canada, representing Metis and non-status Indians, and by the Assembly of First Nations representing status Indians.
The three national organizations are representative of their respective aboriginal peoples, and they should select from among themselves their own representatives at the constitutional conference. It would be inappropriate for the government to select these representatives and even more inappropriate to question whether the aboriginal organizations represent both sexes of their peoples. It is manifestly impossible for the Prime Minister to invite to the constitutional conference every aboriginal organizations with an interest in the Constitution, even though the government might sympathize with their concerns.
As I noted earlier, the Inuit Committee on National Issues has committed itself to allow some time for discussion on women's issues. Let us hope that aboriginal women in Canada can build on this success and obtain from every other aboriginal organization, whether national, provincial or territorial, their agreement to represent more specifically their own interests and concerns.
